modules.title: What runs when Spring Boot starts?
modules.outcome: Explain how main(), the container, configuration, and the web server fit together.
modules.cue: Boot builds the room. Beans are the people inside it.
modules.version: Java 21 · Spring Boot 4.0.3 teaching baseline

sections.title: The idea
sections.content:
# The idea

Spring Boot builds on Spring. Spring manages objects called beans. Boot supplies useful defaults when the required classes and settings are present. This is auto-configuration. It can step aside when you define your own bean.

Your main method starts an application context. The context finds component classes, creates beans, and connects dependencies. A web application also starts an embedded server. A Java object created with new is still an ordinary object; Spring does not manage it automatically.

Start small: one application class, one controller, one request. Keep the main class above your feature packages so component scanning can find them. A green startup log only says startup succeeded. It does not prove every request or database query works.

sections.title: A small example
Follow the execution
sections.content:
# Follow the execution

1. The JVM calls main. Boot builds the context.
2. Component scanning finds PingController. MVC records its /ping mapping.
3. The server listens on the configured port. A request reaches the mapped method.
4. The method returns text. MVC writes the HTTP response.

Command-line properties override application.properties for this simple case. Profiles select environment-specific settings; they are not a place to commit secrets. Use the condition report (--debug) to see why a default was applied.

sections.title: What can go wrong
sections.content:
# What can go wrong

A controller outside the scanned package may never become a bean. A port conflict happens before a request is handled. A 404 after startup is a routing problem, not proof that Boot failed to launch.

**Memory cue:** Boot builds the room. Beans are the people inside it.

Close this lesson. Draw the five steps. Explain one failure in your own words before opening Practice.

exercises.title: Find and fix the bug
exercises.prompt:
# Find and fix the bug

The app starts on 8081. A developer calls localhost:8080/ping and reports that the controller is broken. List two checks before editing the method.

Write: prediction → proposed change → observed evidence → explanation. Run code only in a separate training sandbox. If you did not run it, say so. Submit before opening a reference.
exercises.solution:
# One valid repair

Check the startup log for the listening port, then call 8081/ping. Check that the controller package is below the application package and that the mapping is GET /ping. Separate a connection failure from an HTTP 404.

**How to check:** A 404 means a server handled the request but did not find that resource. Inspect routing and package discovery before changing memory or transactions.

Other repairs are acceptable if they satisfy the stated rule. Explain the failure timeline and show a relevant test. Code length and matching keywords are not evidence.

exercises.title: Change one condition
exercises.prompt:
# Change one condition

Add a /ready endpoint that depends on a fake store bean. Explain why creating that store with new inside the controller changes how it is configured and tested.

Write: prediction → proposed change → observed evidence → explanation. Run code only in a separate training sandbox. If you did not run it, say so. Submit before opening a reference.
exercises.solution:
# One valid adaptation

Inject the store through the constructor. The container chooses its bean and dependencies. A manually created store bypasses those choices. A readiness check should say what it checked; a constant OK does not prove database readiness.

**Explain back:** Boot builds the room. Beans are the people inside it. What changed in the new condition? What would make your answer fail?

modules.title: Beans, constructors, and shared state
modules.outcome: Trace who creates a service and why singleton fields must be safe across requests.
modules.cue: Share services. Pass request data.
modules.version: Java 21 · Spring Boot 4.0.3 teaching baseline

sections.title: The idea
sections.content:
# The idea

Dependency injection means receiving the objects you need instead of finding or creating them inside a method. A constructor makes those needs visible. It also lets a test pass a fake.

The default bean scope is singleton: one instance per application context for that bean definition. It is not one instance for the whole internet. Several request threads can call the same service. A mutable field such as currentUser can leak data between requests. Keep request data in method arguments and local variables.

An interface is useful when it expresses a real boundary, such as sending messages. You do not need an interface for every small class. If two beans satisfy one constructor parameter, choose deliberately with a qualifier or a primary bean. Circular constructors usually signal mixed responsibilities.

sections.title: A small example
Follow the execution
sections.content:
# Follow the execution

The container sees TaskService needs a Notifier. It creates or finds ConsoleNotifier, then supplies it to the constructor. MVC can now call the same TaskService for many requests.

For a unit test, Java calls the constructor directly with a fake. No server or application context is needed. A context test answers a different question: did scanning, profiles, and bean selection wire the real graph correctly?

sections.title: What can go wrong
sections.content:
# What can go wrong

A singleton service with a field named lastTask is shared state. Marking the field volatile does not make a multi-step business operation atomic. Avoid the field when the value belongs to one call.

**Memory cue:** Share services. Pass request data.

Close this lesson. Draw the five steps. Explain one failure in your own words before opening Practice.

exercises.title: Find and fix the bug
exercises.prompt:
# Find and fix the bug

A service writes this.currentUser = user, calls a slow API, then sends a message to this.currentUser. Draw two overlapping calls that send to the wrong user.

Write: prediction → proposed change → observed evidence → explanation. Run code only in a separate training sandbox. If you did not run it, say so. Submit before opening a reference.
exercises.solution:
# One valid repair

Call A stores Alice and waits. B stores Bob. A resumes and reads Bob. Pass user as a local argument into each step; remove the shared field. Test concurrent calls with a controlled barrier, not Thread.sleep guesses.

**How to check:** One context can reuse one service across request threads. Scope does not provide locking or distributed coordination.

Other repairs are acceptable if they satisfy the stated rule. Explain the failure timeline and show a relevant test. Code length and matching keywords are not evidence.

exercises.title: Change one condition
exercises.prompt:
# Change one condition

Add a second Notifier for tests and one for production. Where will selection happen? How will a unit test avoid both profiles?

Write: prediction → proposed change → observed evidence → explanation. Run code only in a separate training sandbox. If you did not run it, say so. Submit before opening a reference.
exercises.solution:
# One valid adaptation

Select beans with explicit configuration, profiles, or a qualifier. For the unit test construct TaskService with a fake directly. Verify the production wiring with a small context test. A mock passing does not prove profile selection.

**Explain back:** Share services. Pass request data. What changed in the new condition? What would make your answer fail?

modules.title: From HTTP input to a useful error
modules.outcome: Trace request binding, validation, service work, and response mapping.
modules.cue: Bind → check → act → reply.
modules.version: Java 21 · Spring Boot 4.0.3 teaching baseline

sections.title: The idea
sections.content:
# The idea

An HTTP endpoint is a boundary. Treat incoming strings and JSON as untrusted input. Binding turns JSON into Java values. Validation checks those values. Authorization checks whether this caller may perform this action. These are separate steps.

Keep controller methods short. Convert input, call a use case, then map its result to an HTTP response. Put reusable business rules in the service. Return DTOs, which are small request/response types, rather than exposing database entities and all their fields.

Choose errors that help the client: bad input is different from a missing record or a conflict. Do not return stack traces or SQL text to callers. An exception handler can make the error shape consistent.

sections.title: A small example
Follow the execution
sections.content:
# Follow the execution

A servlet filter can run before MVC. DispatcherServlet chooses a handler. A message converter reads JSON. Validation runs on the bound input. Then the controller invokes the service. The response converter writes JSON.

Try an empty title, malformed JSON, a valid request, and a simulated service conflict. For each, predict whether the service should run. Use @RestControllerAdvice with @ExceptionHandler for your domain errors. Log a request ID so an operator can find details privately.

sections.title: What can go wrong
sections.content:
# What can go wrong

Returning an entity can trigger lazy queries during JSON serialization or reveal an internal field. A 200 response containing {error: ...} also makes clients guess whether the operation succeeded.

**Memory cue:** Bind → check → act → reply.

Close this lesson. Draw the five steps. Explain one failure in your own words before opening Practice.

exercises.title: Find and fix the bug
exercises.prompt:
# Find and fix the bug

A POST endpoint accepts an empty title, saves an entity, and returns its entire graph. Identify the boundary mistakes and propose response tests.

Write: prediction → proposed change → observed evidence → explanation. Run code only in a separate training sandbox. If you did not run it, say so. Submit before opening a reference.
exercises.solution:
# One valid repair

Validate a request DTO before service work. Return a TaskView with only allowed fields and 201 on creation. Test invalid JSON and blank input yield 400 with no creation; missing resources yield 404; conflicts use a deliberate 409 mapping. Validate service rules too when called outside HTTP.

**How to check:** A service can have more than one caller. Its required business rules cannot depend only on controller validation.

Other repairs are acceptable if they satisfy the stated rule. Explain the failure timeline and show a relevant test. Code length and matching keywords are not evidence.

exercises.title: Change one condition
exercises.prompt:
# Change one condition

A background import calls the same service without HTTP. Which rules must still hold?

Write: prediction → proposed change → observed evidence → explanation. Run code only in a separate training sandbox. If you did not run it, say so. Submit before opening a reference.
exercises.solution:
# One valid adaptation

Business rules belong below the controller. Enforce required task state and ownership in the use case or domain layer. HTTP annotations are one input boundary; a worker must validate its inputs too. Use database constraints for rules that must survive concurrency.

**Explain back:** Bind → check → act → reply. What changed in the new condition? What would make your answer fail?

modules.title: Who are you, and may you do this?
modules.outcome: Separate authentication, ownership checks, CSRF, and CORS.
modules.cue: Login opens the building. Permission opens the room.
modules.version: Java 21 · Spring Boot 4.0.3 teaching baseline

sections.title: The idea
sections.content:
# The idea

Authentication identifies the caller. Authorization decides whether that caller may access this specific task. A logged-in user can still be forbidden from editing another user’s data.

Spring Security usually runs in a servlet filter chain before controller handling. It can authenticate a session or bearer token and attach a security context. Route rules are a first gate. The service still needs object-level rules when it can be called from another route or job.

CORS controls which browser origins can read responses. It is not an ownership check. CSRF protects cookie-authenticated actions from unwanted cross-site requests. Do not disable it merely because the endpoint uses JSON. Decide from the authentication mechanism and browser threat model.

sections.title: A small example
Follow the execution
sections.content:
# Follow the execution

Follow a request with no credentials: the security entry point decides how to challenge or redirect. Follow a valid user requesting somebody else’s task: authentication can succeed while authorization fails.

For API tests, assert response status and that no write occurred. Check session cookie settings, CSRF expectations, and explicit allowed origins separately. Keep secrets and token contents out of logs.

sections.title: What can go wrong
sections.content:
# What can go wrong

A hidden Edit button is not protection. The user can send HTTP directly. A valid JWT proves only the claims you actually verify, including signature, issuer, audience, expiry, and your chosen access rules.

**Memory cue:** Login opens the building. Permission opens the room.

Close this lesson. Draw the five steps. Explain one failure in your own words before opening Practice.

exercises.title: Find and fix the bug
exercises.prompt:
# Find and fix the bug

PUT /tasks/41 accepts ownerId from JSON and uses it to authorize. Explain an attack and a repair.

Write: prediction → proposed change → observed evidence → explanation. Run code only in a separate training sandbox. If you did not run it, say so. Submit before opening a reference.
exercises.solution:
# One valid repair

A caller can send the victim ownerId. Derive identity from the verified security context. Load task 41 within an allowed scope or compare its stored owner with that identity. Return a deliberate forbidden/not-found response and test that the row did not change.

**How to check:** Client-controlled fields are claims, not proof. The server must establish and check identity.

Other repairs are acceptable if they satisfy the stated rule. Explain the failure timeline and show a relevant test. Code length and matching keywords are not evidence.

exercises.title: Change one condition
exercises.prompt:
# Change one condition

The frontend moves to another origin. Does adding it to CORS make users authorized?

Write: prediction → proposed change → observed evidence → explanation. Run code only in a separate training sandbox. If you did not run it, say so. Submit before opening a reference.
exercises.solution:
# One valid adaptation

No. CORS changes browser response access. Keep authentication, object permissions, and CSRF decisions. Non-browser clients are not constrained by browser CORS enforcement.

**Explain back:** Login opens the building. Permission opens the room. What changed in the new condition? What would make your answer fail?

modules.title: JPA: Java objects are not SQL
modules.outcome: Explain entity state, repository queries, lazy reads, and the N+1 problem.
modules.cue: Every object access deserves a SQL question.
modules.version: Java 21 · Spring Boot 4.0.3 teaching baseline

sections.title: The idea
sections.content:
# The idea

JPA maps objects to relational rows. Hibernate is a common implementation. A repository is an access boundary; it does not remove the need to reason about SQL.

An entity loaded inside a persistence context is managed. Changing it can produce an UPDATE when work is flushed. Flush sends SQL; commit makes the transaction durable. They are not the same event. A detached object is no longer tracked by that context.

Associations can hide database work. Reading 20 tasks and then each task.owner.name can issue 21 queries. That is N+1: one list query plus one per item. Choose a fetch plan or a DTO query for this screen. Do not switch every relation to eager loading; that can load a huge graph.

sections.title: A small example
Follow the execution
sections.content:
# Follow the execution

Ask what SQL runs at each line. The repository list call loads task rows. A lazy owner access can trigger another query while the context is open. Outside it, an uninitialized association may fail.

Build the response inside a deliberate read boundary. Count queries with test instrumentation or SQL logs in a sandbox. Compare one item and twenty items. A constant small query count is evidence; the word repository is not.

sections.title: What can go wrong
sections.content:
# What can go wrong

An in-memory H2 test may hide PostgreSQL behavior. SQL logs can also expose values, so use synthetic test data. A uniqueness pre-check without a database constraint can race.

**Memory cue:** Every object access deserves a SQL question.

Close this lesson. Draw the five steps. Explain one failure in your own words before opening Practice.

exercises.title: Find and fix the bug
exercises.prompt:
# Find and fix the bug

A /tasks list works locally but becomes slow with 100 tasks. Each item reads its owner. Explain how to confirm and repair the query count.

Write: prediction → proposed change → observed evidence → explanation. Run code only in a separate training sandbox. If you did not run it, say so. Submit before opening a reference.
exercises.solution:
# One valid repair

Measure SQL count for 1 versus 100 tasks. If it grows by roughly one per task, choose a DTO projection or a fetch join for the required to-one relation. Keep bounded pagination and deterministic ordering. Test query count and response shape, not just list size.

**How to check:** Flush synchronizes changes with the database connection. The transaction can still roll back before commit.

Other repairs are acceptable if they satisfy the stated rule. Explain the failure timeline and show a relevant test. Code length and matching keywords are not evidence.

exercises.title: Change one condition
exercises.prompt:
# Change one condition

Now each task has thousands of comments. Should the task list fetch all comments too?

Write: prediction → proposed change → observed evidence → explanation. Run code only in a separate training sandbox. If you did not run it, say so. Submit before opening a reference.
exercises.solution:
# One valid adaptation

No. Return comment counts or a separate paginated endpoint. A fetch plan serves one use case. To-many joins multiply rows; pagination over those rows can behave unexpectedly. Explain the SQL shape and measure it.

**Explain back:** Every object access deserves a SQL question. What changed in the new condition? What would make your answer fail?

modules.title: Transactions, proxies, and races
modules.outcome: Predict whether a transaction starts and design one test that catches a race.
modules.cue: The wrapper must see the call.
modules.version: Java 21 · Spring Boot 4.0.3 teaching baseline

sections.title: The idea
sections.content:
# The idea

A transaction groups database changes so they commit or roll back together. It does not automatically group a database write with an email or an external API call.

Spring commonly applies @Transactional through a proxy: a wrapper around the real bean. A call that enters through that proxy can start a transaction. Calling this.otherMethod() inside the object usually skips that proxy. Private methods are also unsuitable boundaries for this common setup.

By default, unchecked exceptions and Error trigger rollback; checked exceptions do not unless configured. A caught exception may not escape to the wrapper at all. Also, two valid transactions can still race. Use a database constraint, conditional update, or appropriate lock for the rule you need.

sections.title: A small example
Follow the execution
sections.content:
# Follow the execution

Controller → proxy → begin → service → SQL → commit → return. If an unchecked exception leaves the service, the wrapper rolls back instead.

For a race, draw A reads 1, B reads 1, A writes 0, B writes 0. Both callers may believe they won. A transaction annotation alone does not prevent this lost update. Conditional updates or optimistic version checks turn the second attempt into a visible conflict.

sections.title: What can go wrong
sections.content:
# What can go wrong

A unit test using new CompleteTask(...) bypasses the proxy. It can test business decisions but cannot prove transaction interception. A transaction-wrapped test can also hide a missing production boundary.

**Memory cue:** The wrapper must see the call.

Close this lesson. Draw the five steps. Explain one failure in your own words before opening Practice.

exercises.title: Find and fix the bug
exercises.prompt:
# Find and fix the bug

A public method calls this.reserve(), where reserve alone has @Transactional. The team expects all reservation writes to roll back. What is missing?

Write: prediction → proposed change → observed evidence → explanation. Run code only in a separate training sandbox. If you did not run it, say so. Submit before opening a reference.
exercises.solution:
# One valid repair

The internal call does not cross the usual Spring proxy. Put the public use-case transaction on the externally called bean method, or move reservation into another injected bean with a public transaction boundary. Verify actual rollback with a context/database test after the call ends.

**How to check:** The injected bean reference normally points to the wrapper. A self-call stays on the same target object.

Other repairs are acceptable if they satisfy the stated rule. Explain the failure timeline and show a relevant test. Code length and matching keywords are not evidence.

exercises.title: Change one condition

# Change one condition

Write: prediction → proposed change → observed evidence → explanation. Run code only in a separate training sandbox. If you did not run it, say so. Submit before opening a reference.
exercises.solution:
# One valid adaptation

Write an outbox row with the business change in one DB transaction. A worker retries sending it. The provider may accept a message before a timeout, so retries still need an idempotency strategy or duplicate tolerance. Outbox guarantees saved intent, not universal exactly-once delivery.

**Explain back:** The wrapper must see the call. What changed in the new condition? What would make your answer fail?

sections.title: The idea
sections.content:
# The idea

A unit test checks a small piece of behavior using ordinary objects and controlled dependencies. It should be quick. A web test checks HTTP binding, validation, status, and JSON. An integration test checks actual wiring or external boundaries.

Do not load the entire application for every arithmetic or ownership rule. Do not use only mocks to claim that SQL, transactions, and bean discovery work. Use a small number of database tests against the database type you rely on for concurrency and constraints.

Test observable behavior. A good failure test names what must not happen: a denied request must not write, a failed transaction must not leave half a change, and a duplicate command must not charge twice.

sections.title: A small example
Follow the execution
sections.content:
# Follow the execution

First make the test fail for the right reason. Then change the implementation. For a bug in JSON validation, a service mock alone cannot see the problem; exercise MVC. For a missing unique index, an in-memory repository fake cannot see it; test the database.

Avoid asserting exact private method order when the contract allows alternatives. Control time and remote responses. Race tests need controlled overlap; random sleeps create flaky evidence.

sections.title: What can go wrong
sections.content:
# What can go wrong

A test marked @Transactional may roll back its own work and hide production commit/after-commit behavior. Verify relevant effects after the actual use-case transaction has completed.

**Memory cue:** Test at the layer where the bug can live.

Close this lesson. Draw the five steps. Explain one failure in your own words before opening Practice.

exercises.solution:
# One valid repair

Add a database unique constraint on the true key and a test with two independent transactions attempting that key. Assert one stored row and a deliberate conflict response. A validator pre-check alone races. A Mockito verify call does not test the database rule.

**How to check:** The constraint exists at the database boundary. Test where that rule is enforced.

Other repairs are acceptable if they satisfy the stated rule. Explain the failure timeline and show a relevant test. Code length and matching keywords are not evidence.

**Explain back:** Test at the layer where the bug can live. What changed in the new condition? What would make your answer fail?

sections.title: The idea
sections.content:
# The idea

A useful service needs more than a happy-path endpoint. Ask how it starts, how you know it is healthy, how it behaves when a dependency slows down, and how you undo a release.

Logs explain individual events. Metrics show trends such as error rate and latency. Traces connect work across services. Give every request a correlation ID, but do not log passwords or whole request bodies. A liveness check asks if the process should be restarted. Readiness asks whether it should receive traffic.

Set connection and response timeouts on outbound calls. Retry only failures that can safely be retried. Use limited attempts and backoff. A retry without an idempotency rule may multiply writes. A queue also needs backlog monitoring and a recovery plan.

sections.title: A small example
sections.content:
# A small example

```properties
# Teaching defaults. Expose only the endpoints you actually need.
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info
management.endpoint.health.show-details=never
spring.jpa.open-in-view=false
```

Capstone: build POST /tasks, GET /tasks/{id}, and POST /tasks/{id}/complete in the sandbox. Use request DTOs, a service, persistence, ownership, tests, and a fake notification boundary. Read the SQL count for the list endpoint. Add one failure at a time.

sections.title: Follow the execution
sections.content:
# Follow the execution

Start with a reported symptom: POST /complete takes 12 seconds. Find the request ID, then time the database step and provider step. Check whether timeouts and retries explain the total duration. A bigger thread pool may only increase pressure on the slow dependency.

Release a database change in compatible steps when old and new app versions overlap. Keep a rollback path. A feature flag cannot undo data already deleted. Write a short runbook: symptom, check, safe action, verification.

sections.title: What can go wrong
sections.content:
# What can go wrong

Health endpoints may expose internals if published without access control. Retry loops can create a traffic storm. A benchmark with one request does not measure a saturated connection pool.

**Memory cue:** Observe → isolate → repair → verify.

Close this lesson. Draw the five steps. Explain one failure in your own words before opening Practice.

exercises.title: Find and fix the bug
exercises.prompt:
# Find and fix the bug

A slow provider receives three retries for every request. Traffic doubles and the app stalls. Propose a first safe investigation and a lasting repair.

Write: prediction → proposed change → observed evidence → explanation. Run code only in a separate training sandbox. If you did not run it, say so. Submit before opening a reference.
exercises.solution:
# One valid repair

Measure provider latency, attempt count, queue depth, and thread/connection use. Bound timeouts and retry attempts; retry only safe operations. Use backoff and isolate the failing dependency. Preserve pending intent and expose status rather than blocking indefinitely. Verify with a controlled slow fake.

**How to check:** The provider may have completed the action before the response was lost. Treat the outcome as uncertain.

Other repairs are acceptable if they satisfy the stated rule. Explain the failure timeline and show a relevant test. Code length and matching keywords are not evidence.

**Explain back:** Observe → isolate → repair → verify. What changed in the new condition? What would make your answer fail?

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.content:
## Understand the idea

Configuration changes behavior without changing the application’s source. That makes it powerful and easy to misunderstand. A value may come from a file, profile, environment variable, command line, or remote source. Record the effective value and its source without logging secrets.

Group related settings with typed configuration rather than scattering string lookups. Validate required URLs, limits, and durations at startup. A service that starts with an invalid payment endpoint can fail much later in a confusing place.

Profiles select groups of behavior; they are not a permission system or a secret store. Prefer workload identity for cloud access and explicit secret injection. Test the production-like configuration graph separately from pure business logic.

sections.title: Follow a concrete example
Trace the execution
sections.content:
## Trace the execution

Boot prepares environment properties → binds a settings object → validates it → creates dependent clients → starts serving traffic. A bad required setting should fail at a clear boundary.

In a test, supply an invalid max-attempts and verify startup rejects it. Then verify the intended profile chooses the fake integration. A unit test constructing the settings object does not prove binding/validation wiring.

sections.title: Break it and reason about the repair
sections.content:
## Break it and reason about the repair

A default secret committed to a property file is still a secret. A profile name such as prod does not prove that the right database or network was selected.

**Remember:** Bind it. Validate it. Know where it came from.

exercises.title: Diagnose and repair
exercises.prompt:
## Diagnose and repair

A service silently uses a local URL in production because a property name was misspelled. Improve the configuration contract.

Before opening a reference, write your prediction, the exact change, how you would verify it, and why it works. Use synthetic data and a separate lab. State clearly which checks you actually ran.
exercises.solution:
## One valid repair

Use typed grouped configuration, required-value validation, and a wiring test with production-like property names. Expose safe diagnostic metadata, not credentials. Avoid permissive fallback for a setting that must be supplied.

A different answer can work if it meets the stated rule. Explain the failure timeline and the tradeoff. A product name or a longer answer is not proof.

The same container image runs in staging and production. What should differ?

Before opening a reference, write your prediction, the exact change, how you would verify it, and why it works. Use synthetic data and a separate lab. State clearly which checks you actually ran.
exercises.solution:
## One valid transfer

Inject environment-specific endpoints, identities, and secrets at runtime while keeping a reproducible image. Validate each environment’s configuration and permissions. Do not rebuild a secret into separate images.

A different answer can work if it meets the stated rule. Explain the failure timeline and the tradeoff. A product name or a longer answer is not proof.

modules.title: REST contracts: pages, retries, and useful conflicts
modules.outcome: Design bounded APIs and idempotent command handling with explicit retry behavior.
modules.useCase: Ticket creation, payment-like commands, and large operational lists.
modules.benefits: Predictable retries and manageable data loads.
modules.drawbacks: Keys, retention, and mutable list ordering need explicit product rules.
modules.version: Java 21 · Spring Boot 4.0.3 teaching baseline
modules.cue: A retry is the same command only when you can identify it.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.content:
## Understand the idea

An endpoint contract includes more than a URL. Define allowed input, authorization, response shape, errors, ordering, page limits, and retry semantics. A list without a bound can turn an ordinary screen into an accidental bulk export.

Use stable ordering for pagination. Offset pages can shift when rows are inserted; a cursor can be more stable for an append-heavy feed. A cursor must still be scoped to the caller and filter contract.

A retried create can duplicate a ticket. An idempotency key identifies one logical command. Store the key with a request fingerprint and result under a database uniqueness rule. The same key with a different request should conflict. A pre-check in a local map does not protect multiple service instances.

sections.title: Follow a concrete example
sections.content:
## Follow a concrete example

```text
POST /tickets
Idempotency-Key: client-generated-command-id
Body: {title, workspaceId}

DB transaction:
  claim unique (actor_scope, command_key)
  compare request fingerprint if already claimed
  create ticket and store response identity
  commit
```

For GET /tickets?after=...&limit=..., cap limit on the server and use a deterministic ordered key. Tokens are data, not authorization.

sections.title: Trace the execution
sections.content:
## Trace the execution

A creates a ticket and commits, but the response is lost. A retry with the same key reads the saved result rather than creating a second ticket. A different payload with that key receives a deliberate conflict.

Test simultaneous same-key requests, a timeout after commit, an invalid cursor, and permission changes. Define key retention; forgetting keys eventually changes retry behavior.

sections.title: Break it and reason about the repair
sections.content:
## Break it and reason about the repair

PUT/POST method names alone do not implement idempotence. Cursor encoding is not encryption or access control. A 200 containing an error object confuses clients.

**Remember:** A retry is the same command only when you can identify it.

exercises.title: Diagnose and repair
exercises.prompt:
## Diagnose and repair

Two instances both see no idempotency key and create separate rows. Repair the race.

Before opening a reference, write your prediction, the exact change, how you would verify it, and why it works. Use synthetic data and a separate lab. State clearly which checks you actually ran.
exercises.solution:
## One valid repair

Enforce a unique scoped command key in the database and handle the winner/loser under a clear transaction contract. Store or reconstruct the accepted result and reject conflicting fingerprints. Test independent concurrent transactions.

A different answer can work if it meets the stated rule. Explain the failure timeline and the tradeoff. A product name or a longer answer is not proof.

exercises.solution:
## One valid transfer

Rows can move across the cursor boundary. Define snapshot/session semantics or accept and explain possible duplicates/misses, using a stable tie-breaker. If the product requires a stable export, use a snapshot/export job rather than pretending a live list is frozen.

A different answer can work if it meets the stated rule. Explain the failure timeline and the tradeoff. A product name or a longer answer is not proof.

modules.title: SQL plans, connection pools, and transaction size
modules.outcome: Investigate a slow service without assuming more threads or caching is the first fix.
modules.useCase: Slow list endpoints and connection exhaustion incidents.
modules.benefits: Repairs the bottleneck rather than hiding it.
modules.drawbacks: Representative measurement and safe database change plans take effort.
modules.version: Java 21 · Spring Boot 4.0.3 teaching baseline
modules.cue: Find the wait before adding capacity.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.content:
## Understand the idea

A request can wait for a connection, a row lock, a slow query, or an external service. Low CPU does not prove spare useful capacity. Trace waiting time separately from execution time.

An index should serve a query shape: filter, ordering, and selected data. Check the plan with representative synthetic data and actual predicates. An index adds write/storage cost and may not help a very broad query. Avoid loading full entities when a screen needs a few fields.

A connection pool is a limit, not free throughput. Long transactions hold connections and sometimes locks. Increasing web threads beyond database capacity can grow queues and latency. Keep network calls out of database lock windows when possible.

sections.title: Follow a concrete example
sections.content:
## Follow a concrete example

```sql
-- A common bounded work queue query:
SELECT id, title FROM tickets
WHERE workspace_id = 7 AND status = 'open'
ORDER BY created_at, id LIMIT 50;
-- Investigate a matching composite index and EXPLAIN on training data.
```

Use PostgreSQL for PostgreSQL plan/lock claims. The existing H2 lab proves smaller contracts, not the production engine’s plan or concurrency behavior.

sections.title: Trace the execution
sections.content:
## Trace the execution

Trace request arrival → pool wait → SQL/lock wait → row fetch → DTO mapping → response. Measure each boundary before changing a limit.

For a transaction that calls a slow provider between writes, show how many requests can hold connections while waiting. Move delivery intent into an outbox when a later external effect is acceptable.

sections.title: Break it and reason about the repair
sections.content:
## Break it and reason about the repair

A larger pool can overload the database. SQL logs can expose values. A query that is fast on 10 rows may use a different plan on a million.

**Remember:** Find the wait before adding capacity.

exercises.title: Diagnose and repair
exercises.prompt:
## Diagnose and repair

The app has 200 web threads and 10 DB connections, with 20-second provider calls inside transactions. Explain the likely queue and a repair.

Before opening a reference, write your prediction, the exact change, how you would verify it, and why it works. Use synthetic data and a separate lab. State clearly which checks you actually ran.
exercises.solution:
## One valid repair

Requests can hold scarce connections while waiting on the provider. Measure pool wait, transaction duration, and provider latency. Shorten the transaction, persist intent, and move safe external work after it. Tune limits from database capacity, not thread count alone.

A different answer can work if it meets the stated rule. Explain the failure timeline and the tradeoff. A product name or a longer answer is not proof.

exercises.title: Change the situation
exercises.prompt:
## Change the situation

A new index speeds reads but slows a bulk import. How do you assess the tradeoff?

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.content:
## Understand the idea

A remote call crosses a failure boundary. The provider can reject, respond slowly, complete and lose the response, or return malformed data. A timeout says you did not get an answer in time; it does not prove no side effect occurred.

Choose connection/response timeouts and an overall request budget. Limit attempts and use backoff with jitter where appropriate. Retry only failures and operations whose semantics allow it. A circuit breaker can stop repeated pressure on a failing dependency; it does not repair correctness or replace a timeout.

Keep an adapter around the provider so your use case works with a small result contract. Record correlation ID, logical command key, attempt number, duration, and outcome category without logging secrets or whole payloads.

sections.title: Follow a concrete example
Trace the execution
sections.content:
## Trace the execution

Business change commits with a receipt intent. A worker sends it with eventKey E. The provider accepts E but the response is lost. A retry uses E again under the provider’s documented key contract, or reconciliation resolves uncertainty when such a contract is absent.

Do not retry an entire use case if that repeats unrelated writes. Put the retry around the boundary you actually intend to repeat.

sections.title: Break it and reason about the repair
sections.content:
## Break it and reason about the repair

Nested retries multiply attempts. A 3-attempt client inside a 3-attempt job can make nine calls. A fallback that reports success without performing the required effect is a false result.

**Remember:** Bound the wait. Identify the command. Admit uncertainty.

exercises.solution:

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.content:
## Understand the idea

A use case names an action, such as AssignTicket. It receives validated intent and a trusted actor, checks the rule, coordinates persistence, and returns a result. A controller translates HTTP into that action. A scheduled job can call the same use case through a different entry point.

Put rules near the data and behavior they govern. Do not let a REST controller become the only place ownership is checked if a job or another controller can bypass it. Keep adapters small around SQL and remote services when those boundaries need independent tests.

More interfaces do not automatically mean better architecture. Use a seam when it reduces a real coupling or gives a useful test/failure boundary. Start with a modular monolith when independent deployment is not needed; a network adds partial failure and operations work.

sections.title: Follow a concrete example
sections.content:
## Follow a concrete example

```text
ticket/http/AssignController.java   parse + response mapping
ticket/application/AssignTicket.java  trusted actor + transaction
ticket/domain/AssignmentPolicy.java   allowed transition
ticket/persistence/TaskRepository.java SQL access
ticket/integration/ReceiptGateway.java remote boundary
```

Keep module dependencies one-way. Do not expose every entity field as a public API just to save a DTO.

sections.title: Trace the execution
sections.content:
## Trace the execution

For a new requirement, identify which boundary changes. A new HTTP representation need not rewrite the domain rule. A new provider should mostly change an adapter if its semantics fit the existing contract.

modules.title: Integration tests, migrations, and a release rehearsal
modules.outcome: Prove the deployed configuration, database changes, and failure recovery beyond mock tests.
modules.useCase: A service release with a schema change and background delivery.
modules.benefits: Makes deployment assumptions testable.
modules.drawbacks: Integration environments cost time and still do not cover every production condition.
modules.version: Java 21 · Spring Boot 4.0.3 teaching baseline
modules.cue: Test the boundary. Rehearse the release. Separate data recovery.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.content:
## Understand the idea

A unit suite can pass while the real application has the wrong bean, migration, permission, or SQL behavior. Keep focused integration tests for the boundaries you rely on. Use a disposable real database when engine behavior matters.

A release changes code, configuration, and sometimes data. Old and new instances may overlap. A migration should remain compatible during that overlap. A code rollback does not restore deleted data or unsend messages.

Rehearse a small release with a known failure. Observe readiness, startup migration ownership, graceful shutdown, in-flight requests, and a rollback decision. A runbook is a short path from symptom to check to safe action to verification.

sections.title: Follow a concrete example
sections.content:
## Follow a concrete example

```text
Release rehearsal
1. Start old app against synthetic database.
2. Apply compatible schema expansion once.
3. Start new app and verify critical paths.
4. Simulate provider slowdown and one denied action.
5. Stop new app; verify old app still reads the expanded schema.
6. Record data effects that a code rollback does not reverse.
```

Do not let every app replica independently run a risky long backfill on startup.

sections.title: Trace the execution
sections.content:
## Trace the execution

Build an immutable artifact → verify its configuration → apply a deliberate migration → start and check readiness → send a smoke request → observe → promote or roll back. Keep migration execution separate from ordinary request scaling.

Tests should show both permitted and denied behavior, transaction rollback, and an adapter failure. A green health endpoint alone does not prove the feature works.

sections.title: Break it and reason about the repair
sections.content:
## Break it and reason about the repair

Tests wrapped in a transaction can hide after-commit behavior. A fake repository cannot prove a unique index. A rollback button cannot undo every data effect.

**Remember:** Test the boundary. Rehearse the release. Separate data recovery.

modules.title: Values, names, and surprising mutation
modules.outcome: Predict Ruby truthiness and explain when two names share one object.
modules.cue: Names point. Objects change.
modules.version: Ruby 2.7.8 · Rails 4.2.11.3 · Sidekiq 5.2

sections.title: The idea
sections.content:
# The idea

A Ruby variable holds a reference to an object. Assignment copies the reference, not the whole object. If two names point to one array, changing that array is visible through both names. Reassigning one name points it somewhere else.

Only nil and false are false in a Ruby condition. Zero, an empty string, and an empty array are true. This matters when a setting can legitimately be false. settings[:enabled] || true destroys that false value. fetch(:enabled, true) uses a default only when the key is absent.

Symbols are often labels, such as :status. Strings hold text. Neither is magic security. Prefer clear names and small methods over clever one-liners. The old language book discusses Fixnum and Bignum; Ruby 2.7 presents their unified public class as Integer.

sections.title: A small example
sections.content:
# A small example

```ruby
first = ["open"]
second = first
second << "done"
p first                    # ["open", "done"]
second = ["closed"]
p first                    # still ["open", "done"]

settings = { enabled: false }
p settings[:enabled] || true # true: the false value was lost
p settings.fetch(:enabled, true) # false

buckets = Hash.new { |h, key| h[key] = [] }
buckets[:today] << "task-1"
p buckets[:tomorrow]        # []: a different array
```

sections.title: Follow the execution
sections.content:
# Follow the execution

Draw two arrows to the same array before the append. After second is reassigned, draw its arrow to a new array. The first arrow did not move.

Hash.new([]) uses one shared default object and does not insert missing keys when you read them. The block form above creates and stores a separate array for each new key. dup copies only one level; nested arrays can still be shared.

sections.title: What can go wrong
sections.content:
# What can go wrong

A method ending in ! often warns about a surprising or dangerous variant; it is not a universal promise of mutation. Read the method contract. freeze is also shallow unless you freeze nested objects yourself.

**Memory cue:** Names point. Objects change.

Close this lesson. Draw the five steps. Explain one failure in your own words before opening Practice.

exercises.prompt:

exercises.solution:
# One valid repair

Use config.fetch(:send_email, true) to preserve false. Use Hash.new { |h,k| h[k] = [] } for separate stored buckets. Test missing, false, and true settings. Test two distinct bucket keys and inspect keys as well as values.

**How to check:** Zero and empty containers are truthy in Ruby. Test presence and numeric rules explicitly.

Other repairs are acceptable if they satisfy the stated rule. Explain the failure timeline and show a relevant test. Code length and matching keywords are not evidence.

exercises.prompt:
# Change one condition

You dup a hash containing an array, then append to the copied array. What happens to the original? How would you avoid shared nested state?

Write: prediction → proposed change → observed evidence → explanation. Run code only in a separate training sandbox. If you did not run it, say so. Submit before opening a reference.
exercises.solution:
# One valid adaptation

A shallow dup still references the same nested array, so the original sees the append. Copy the specific nested structure you intend to edit, or create immutable value objects and new values. Do not assume a universal deep copy works for every object.

**Explain back:** Names point. Objects change. What changed in the new condition? What would make your answer fail?

modules.title: Enumerable: choose the shape of the result
modules.outcome: Use each, map, select, find, and reduce without hiding side effects.
modules.cue: Map changes shape inside. Select changes who stays.
modules.version: Ruby 2.7.8 · Rails 4.2.11.3 · Sidekiq 5.2

sections.title: The idea
sections.content:
# The idea

A block is a chunk of behavior passed to a method. Enumerable gives collections common operations. Choose by the result you need: each for an action, map for one output per input, select for a subset, find for one match, and reduce for an accumulated result.

Do not memorize these as interchangeable loops. Ask what shape should come back. map preserves the number of items, even if your block returns nil. select keeps original items whose block result is truthy. each normally returns the receiver, not the block results.

Enumerable over an array runs Ruby code now. An ActiveRecord relation can build SQL lazily. relation.select(:id) and array.select { ... } do different work. Check the receiver before guessing from a method name.

sections.title: A small example
sections.content:
# A small example

```ruby
tasks = [{id: 1, done: false}, {id: 2, done: true}]
ids = tasks.map { |task| task[:id] }           # [1, 2]
open_tasks = tasks.select { |task| !task[:done] }
first_done = tasks.find { |task| task[:done] } # the second hash
count = tasks.reduce(0) { |n, task| n + (task[:done] ? 1 : 0) }

def with_note
  puts "before"
  yield "task-1"
  puts "after"
end
with_note { |id| puts id }
```

sections.title: Follow the execution
sections.content:
# Follow the execution

For map, write the block result below each input. For select, write keep/drop below each input. For reduce, write the accumulator after each step.

yield calls the provided block. A method that may be called without one can check block_given?. An Enumerator can defer iteration. lazy can avoid creating intermediate arrays, but the work still happens when a terminal operation asks for results.

sections.title: What can go wrong
sections.content:
# What can go wrong

Using map only to send messages communicates the wrong intent and allocates an unused array. A query followed by Ruby select can load far more database rows than a SQL where clause.

**Memory cue:** Map changes shape inside. Select changes who stays.

Close this lesson. Draw the five steps. Explain one failure in your own words before opening Practice.

# Find and fix the bug

exercises.solution:
# One valid repair

It returns one value per input, including nil for every false branch. Use select { |t| t[:done] } to filter, then map if you need IDs. Test the result contents and size with both done and open tasks.

**How to check:** select filters original items. map transforms every item into a block result.

Other repairs are acceptable if they satisfy the stated rule. Explain the failure timeline and show a relevant test. Code length and matching keywords are not evidence.

sections.title: The idea
sections.content:
# The idea

Every ordinary Ruby method call has a receiver. self is the current receiver. An instance method lives on a class or module; each instance supplies its own instance variables. A class is also an object, so def self.build defines a singleton method on that class object.

include adds a module to instance-method lookup. extend adds module methods to one object’s singleton lookup. prepend puts a module before the class, so a wrapper can call super to continue the chain. Order matters.

Class variables written @@name can be shared across an inheritance tree in surprising ways. A class instance variable written @name on the class object is different from an instance variable on an instance. Avoid shared mutable class state when the value belongs to one request.

sections.title: A small example
sections.content:
# A small example

```ruby
module Audit
  def label
    "audit(" + super + ")"
  end
end
class Task
  def label; "task"; end
end
Task.prepend(Audit)
p Task.new.label      # "audit(task)"
p Task.ancestors      # inspect the lookup path
p Task.new.method(:label).owner # Audit
```

Try include instead of prepend in a disposable Ruby file. Predict the owner before running it. The language book predates prepend; use the Ruby 2.7 docs for that addition.

sections.title: Follow the execution
sections.content:
# Follow the execution

For prepend, begin at the wrapper module. Its super calls the next matching implementation, Task#label. With include, the class method normally wins before the included module.

To debug a surprising method, inspect obj.method(:name).owner and .source_location. Inspect Class.ancestors for included/prepended modules. This turns “Ruby magic” into a path you can follow.

sections.title: What can go wrong
sections.content:
# What can go wrong

A concern can quietly add callbacks and class methods. Naming a module does not isolate its side effects. A singleton method defined on one object does not automatically become an instance method for every object.

**Memory cue:** Follow the receiver, then the lookup path.

sections.title: The idea
sections.content:
# The idea

A closure carries access to variables from its surrounding scope. It does not take a frozen snapshot of every value. If that variable changes, the closure can see the new value. This is useful for callbacks and risky for long-lived captured state.

A lambda behaves like a small method: it checks argument count more strictly and return leaves the lambda. A non-lambda proc can return from the method where it was defined; after that method has ended, such a return can raise LocalJumpError. Use lambdas when you want method-like callback behavior.

Ruby 2.7 is a transition version for keyword arguments. Code that forwards a final hash as keywords may warn there and fail on Ruby 3. Be explicit about positional arguments, keyword arguments, and a block.

sections.title: A small example
sections.content:
# A small example

```ruby
def create_task(title, urgent: false)
  [title, urgent]
end
def forward(*args, **kwargs, &block)
  create_task(*args, **kwargs, &block)
end
p forward("ship", urgent: true) # ["ship", true]

label = "old"
reader = -> { label }
label = "new"
p reader.call                  # "new"

double = ->(n) { n * 2 }
p double.call(3)                # 6
```

sections.title: Follow the execution
sections.content:
# Follow the execution

Split the call into three envelopes: positional values in args, named values in kwargs, behavior in block. Forward each explicitly. In Ruby 2.7, warnings are useful migration signals; do not silence them without understanding the call shape.

For the closure, reader keeps access to the label binding. Reassignment changes what that binding points to. For a snapshot of text, create a separate value deliberately, such as label.dup.freeze when a shallow frozen string is what you need.

sections.title: What can go wrong
sections.content:
# What can go wrong

A callback with return inside Proc.new may exit its defining method rather than only finishing the callback. Rescue does not make confusing control flow easier to maintain.

sections.title: The idea
sections.content:
# The idea

Rescue exceptions where you can add useful context or recover. Do not turn every failure into nil. rescue without an explicit class normally catches StandardError; it does not mean every possible process failure. Catching Exception broadly can swallow interrupts and system exits.

Use block forms for files so cleanup happens when the block finishes, including on ordinary exceptions. ensure is useful for cleanup, but a return in ensure can accidentally replace the original result or failure.

Bundler selects gem versions from a Gemfile and lockfile. bundle exec runs under that dependency selection. An installed global gem is not proof of what an application uses. Ruby threads can overlap I/O. MRI’s global VM lock limits parallel Ruby execution for CPU-bound work; it is not a database lock or a guarantee against races.

sections.title: A small example
sections.content:
# A small example

```ruby
require "json"
def read_settings(path)
  File.open(path, "r") { |file| JSON.parse(file.read) }
rescue JSON::ParserError => error
  raise ArgumentError, "settings are not valid JSON: #{error.class}"
end

require "minitest/autorun"
class SettingTest < Minitest::Test
  def test_false_is_preserved
    assert_equal false, { enabled: false }.fetch(:enabled, true)
  end
end
```

Run the supplied standalone Ruby lab in the learning journal, not in the work project. It needs only the Ruby standard library.

sections.title: Follow the execution
sections.content:
# Follow the execution

Classify the failure: missing file, invalid JSON, or valid but wrong settings shape. They are different contracts. The block closes the file. The rescue above handles only invalid JSON; it leaves missing-file behavior visible to the caller.

Write one test for a valid input, one malformed input, and one legitimate false value. A unit test can prove the parser contract. It cannot prove Rails boot, Sidekiq delivery, or production permissions.

sections.title: What can go wrong
sections.content:
# What can go wrong

Logging the whole settings file may leak secrets. Tests should use synthetic temporary files. A retry around a non-idempotent side effect can repeat work after a timeout.

**Memory cue:** Catch what you can explain. Test what you can observe.

Close this lesson. Draw the five steps. Explain one failure in your own words before opening Practice.

**How to check:** Bundler uses the project’s dependency definitions and lockfile to resolve gems for that command.

sections.title: The idea
sections.content:
# The idea

Rails connects a Rack request to a route, a controller action, model work, and a response. A before_action can establish a current user. It does not automatically limit every database lookup to that user.

Strong parameters select attributes allowed for mass assignment. They do not authorize access to a particular row. Scope the lookup to the caller’s allowed records, then check action permissions. A service object is an ordinary Ruby object that can organize one use case without making the controller or model do everything.

The work baseline is Rails 4.2: use params.require(...).permit(...), not modern params.expect. ApplicationRecord is a later convention; models here can inherit ActiveRecord::Base. These version differences are part of the lesson, not typos.

sections.title: A small example
sections.content:
# A small example

```ruby
# Teaching fragments; authentication and associations must be configured.
class TasksController < ApplicationController
  before_action :require_user
  def update
    task = current_user.tasks.find(params[:id])
    if task.update(task_params)
      render json: { id: task.id, title: task.title }
    else
      render json: { errors: task.errors.full_messages }, status: 422
    end
  end
  private
  def task_params
    params.require(:task).permit(:title)
  end
end
```

The example assumes current_user is trustworthy and tasks is the allowed ownership scope. A real app may use a policy/ability layer as well.

sections.title: Follow the execution
sections.content:
# Follow the execution

Trace PUT /tasks/7: route chooses update; authentication runs; the scoped find either returns an allowed task or raises not found; permitted input reaches update; the action chooses JSON and status.

The private helper cannot be called as a public action. Use request tests for missing authentication, another user’s ID, rejected attributes, validation errors, and a successful update. Also assert the database row stayed unchanged on rejection.

sections.content:
# What can go wrong

Task.find(params[:id]) plus permit(:title) still allows an ownership bug. Strong parameters protect allowed attributes, not which task you can edit. Never permit owner_id just because the browser sent it.

sections.title: The idea
sections.content:
# The idea

An ActiveRecord relation is a description of a query. where, order, and limit can build it. Iteration often executes it. Once you call to_a, later filtering is usually Ruby work over loaded rows.

Associations can issue queries too. A list of tasks followed by task.owner.name can create one extra query for each task. Preloading brings the required owners in a bounded set of queries. includes may choose different SQL strategies depending on how the relation is used. Inspect the actual SQL instead of assuming a fixed count.

For large lists, choose a stable order and bounded pages. pluck reads selected column values without building full model objects. find_each batches records but has version-specific ordering behavior; do not use it when its order conflicts with a user-facing sequence.

sections.title: A small example
sections.content:
# A small example

```ruby
tasks = Task.where(done: false).order(:id).limit(20)
# No iteration yet: this is a relation.
tasks = tasks.preload(:owner)
rows = tasks.map { |task| [task.id, task.owner.name] }

ids = Task.where(done: false).limit(20).pluck(:id)
```

Use synthetic data and SQL instrumentation in a separate sandbox. Do not paste production rows into notes or AI chat. The precise number of queries depends on association shape and query strategy.

sections.title: Follow the execution
sections.content:
# Follow the execution

Draw the relation-building calls before the first SQL. Then draw the initial task query and the association-loading query. With a simple belongs_to preload, adding more tasks should not add one owner query per task.

Compare one task and twenty tasks. Confirm the response needs each loaded field. An association cache on already loaded objects can make a repeated access look cheap; start the measurement with fresh records.

sections.title: What can go wrong
sections.content:
# What can go wrong

Calling size, count, and length can have different SQL behavior depending on loaded state. A Ruby block passed to select after loading does not become a SQL WHERE clause.

**Memory cue:** Build the query. Ask for rows. Count the SQL.

sections.title: The idea
sections.content:
# The idea

A model validation gives readable feedback before a save. A database constraint protects stored data even when two requests race or a different code path writes the table. Use both when the rule matters.

For example, task keys unique within a workspace need a composite unique index on workspace_id and key. Decide how blank values and case differences should behave. PostgreSQL NULL and collation rules are part of that decision. Do not assume the model and database interpret values identically.

A migration changes shared data structures. Think about existing rows and overlapping application versions. Adding a non-null column to a populated table requires a plan for those rows. A reversible migration method does not mean every business data change is safely reversible.

sections.title: A small example
sections.content:
# A small example

```ruby
# Rails 4.2 style.
class Task < ActiveRecord::Base
  validates :key, presence: true,
    uniqueness: { scope: :workspace_id }
end
class AddTaskKeyIndex < ActiveRecord::Migration
  def change
    add_index :tasks, [:workspace_id, :key], unique: true
  end
end
```

Before creating the index, check and resolve existing duplicates in a safe migration plan. For large production tables, study PostgreSQL concurrent index creation and the Rails 4.2 transaction settings; the short fragment above is a teaching migration, not an online rollout recipe.

sections.title: Follow the execution
sections.content:
# Follow the execution

Two transactions can both pass a uniqueness validator before either inserts. The unique index makes only one conflicting insert succeed. The losing code must handle the database error and return a useful result.

For a rename, use expand → backfill → switch reads/writes → remove old data later. Verify both versions work during deployment. Test the migration on a disposable database with old-shaped data.

sections.title: What can go wrong
sections.content:
# What can go wrong

update_all bypasses model callbacks and validations. That can be useful for a deliberate batch update, but database constraints still apply. A rollback that drops a filled column destroys values.

**Memory cue:** Validation explains. Constraint enforces.

Close this lesson. Draw the five steps. Explain one failure in your own words before opening Practice.

sections.title: The idea
sections.content:
# The idea

Metaprogramming means code that defines or changes program behavior, often methods. Rails uses it to build readable APIs. Start by locating the generated methods rather than assuming the behavior is unknowable.

define_method installs an instance method using a block. define_singleton_method installs one on a particular object. class_eval changes the class/module context; instance_eval changes self for a block. String evaluation also parses code and can be dangerous with outside input. Prefer ordinary methods or explicit tables when they are clearer.

method_missing handles failed lookup. If you deliberately support dynamic methods, implement respond_to_missing? too. Never use an arbitrary request string as a method name to call. public_send restricts visibility, but an allowlist is still needed.

sections.title: A small example
sections.content:
# A small example

```ruby
class TaskPresenter
  LABELS = { open: "Open", done: "Done" }.freeze
  LABELS.each do |state, text|
    define_method("#{state}_label") { text }
  end
end
p TaskPresenter.new.done_label # "Done"

COMMANDS = { "preview" => -> { "preview only" } }.freeze
def run_command(name)
  command = COMMANDS.fetch(name) { raise ArgumentError, "unknown command" }
  command.call
end
```

Use obj.method(:done_label).source_location and .owner to locate the definition. This is a small internal DSL: a limited language for declaring labels.

sections.title: Follow the execution
sections.content:
# Follow the execution

The class body runs as Ruby code. It iterates over LABELS and adds two instance methods. Calling done_label then uses normal method lookup. No generated source string is needed.

For a Rails concern or DSL, ask four questions: when does this declaration run, which object is self, which methods get defined, and which hooks are registered? Trace one declaration all the way to a runtime call.

sections.title: The idea
sections.content:
# The idea

Use a service object to name one business action, such as ReserveStock. Use a transaction when its database changes must commit together. A service object by itself supplies no transaction, retry, or permission guarantee.

save returns false when validations fail. save! raises, which can make a failure visible to the transaction boundary. An ordinary false result is not automatically a rollback of earlier successful writes. ActiveRecord::Rollback requests a rollback without propagating like an ordinary error from the transaction block.

after_commit runs after a successful database commit. It avoids publishing from a transaction that later rolls back. It still leaves a gap: the process can crash after commit and before enqueue. A transactional outbox stores delivery intent with the change, then a worker dispatches it.

sections.title: A small example
sections.content:
# A small example

```ruby
class ReserveStock
  def call(stock_id)
    Stock.transaction do
      stock = Stock.lock.find(stock_id)
      raise "out of stock" unless stock.quantity > 0
      stock.update!(quantity: stock.quantity - 1)
      Reservation.create!(stock_id: stock.id)
      # Optional outbox row belongs in this same transaction.
    end
  end
end
```

The lock serializes competing writes to that row while the transaction runs. It does not serialize all inventory worldwide. Keep slow network calls outside the row-lock window.

sections.title: Follow the execution
sections.content:
# Follow the execution

A enters the transaction and locks the stock row. B waits for that row. A checks and writes, then commits. B continues and sees the new quantity before deciding. Test with independent connections so the overlap is real.

Callbacks are hidden control flow. A concern can install one when included. Draw callback order and side effects before moving them. A clear use-case method often makes orchestration easier to test.

sections.title: What can go wrong
sections.content:
# What can go wrong

Catching an exception inside the transaction and continuing may commit earlier work. Nested transactions are not necessarily independent commits. Read savepoint behavior before promising that an inner rollback undoes everything.

**Memory cue:** One rule. One boundary. One failure timeline.

Close this lesson. Draw the five steps. Explain one failure in your own words before opening Practice.

exercises.solution:
# One valid repair

Use bang writes or explicitly raise/rollback on false. Validate the stock rule under a suitable lock or atomic update. Assert that a stock failure leaves no reservation. Ensure the failure is not swallowed inside the transaction. Test the final database state after the boundary.

**How to check:** A false validation result is ordinary control flow unless the caller turns it into a rollback or exception.

Other repairs are acceptable if they satisfy the stated rule. Explain the failure timeline and show a relevant test. Code length and matching keywords are not evidence.

sections.title: The idea
sections.content:
# The idea

A background job runs later and may run more than once. Pass small JSON-friendly arguments, usually IDs, rather than whole model objects. The row may have changed or disappeared before the worker starts.

Sidekiq 5 uses include Sidekiq::Worker for a direct worker. Modern Sidekiq examples can use newer APIs; keep that version difference visible. A successful enqueue is not proof that work completed. Monitor queue latency, retries, and terminal failures.

Idempotent means repeating the same logical command does not create another logical effect. A seen? pre-check can race. Use a database uniqueness rule for local effects and a stable provider idempotency key when the remote API supports it. A cache stores a copy; define its key, expiry, and invalidation. Tenant/user context may belong in the key.

sections.title: A small example
sections.content:
# A small example

```ruby
# Rails/Sidekiq teaching fragment, not the standalone Ruby lab.
class TaskReceiptWorker
  include Sidekiq::Worker
  sidekiq_options retry: 5
  def perform(task_id, event_key)
    task = Task.find_by(id: task_id)
    return unless task
    ReceiptSender.new.call(task, event_key)
  end
end
# After a deliberate commit/outbox boundary:
# TaskReceiptWorker.perform_async(task.id, event_key)
```

ReceiptSender must define duplicate handling. A unique local sent row alone cannot atomically prove a remote send happened. Use a provider key or reconciliation for that gap.

sections.title: Follow the execution
sections.content:
# Follow the execution

Trace enqueue → delayed start → load current row → attempt external effect → timeout → retry. The timeout does not say whether the provider accepted the action. Reusing the same logical key lets a supporting provider deduplicate it.

For a cache, trace miss → compute → store → hit → underlying update → expiry/invalidation. Record what maximum staleness the user can accept. A permission decision should not use an indefinitely stale shared cache.

sections.title: What can go wrong
sections.content:
# What can go wrong

Testing Sidekiq inline changes timing and can hide a transaction visibility bug. Enqueueing before commit can let a worker read data that is not committed yet. A cache key without tenant scope can leak another tenant’s result.

**Memory cue:** Later means changed. Retry means repeat.

Close this lesson. Draw the five steps. Explain one failure in your own words before opening Practice.

# One valid repair

Use a unique logical event key and durable job/outbox state. Claim local work with a database-safe operation. Send with a stable remote idempotency key if supported. A crash after provider acceptance but before local acknowledgement can still duplicate without that support; reconcile or tolerate duplicates explicitly.

**How to check:** Jobs cross a time/process boundary. Simple serialized arguments and deliberate reload behavior make that boundary clearer.

Other repairs are acceptable if they satisfy the stated rule. Explain the failure timeline and show a relevant test. Code length and matching keywords are not evidence.

sections.title: The idea
sections.content:
# The idea

Start a legacy feature investigation at its entry point. Find the route, controller action, service, model/query, callbacks, worker, and response presenter. Draw only the path relevant to the reported behavior. Search for callers before changing a method contract.

Rails 4.2 uses classic autoloading. File paths, constant names, and development reload behavior matter. Modern Zeitwerk rules cannot be pasted in as if they already run here. Concerns can install callbacks; a method body alone may not show the whole action.

Use model tests for domain rules, request/controller tests for the HTTP boundary, and job/service tests for failure and duplicate handling. The course examples are new task-tracker examples informed by broad patterns such as services, concerns, SQL boundaries, and workers. No private work code or real data belongs in these lessons or AI chat.

sections.title: A small example
sections.content:
# A small example

```ruby
# A small ordinary Ruby service can be tested without Rails.
class CompleteTask
  def initialize(repository)
    @repository = repository
  end
  def call(id)
    task = @repository.fetch(id)
    return :already_done if task[:done]
    @repository.mark_done(id)
    :completed
  end
end
```

This unit seam teaches behavior, not transaction safety. The capstone also needs database and request tests in a separate training app. Use synthetic rows. Never run course commands in the work repository.

sections.title: Follow the execution
sections.content:
# Follow the execution

Capstone: a task can be completed by an allowed member. It creates a receipt intent once. A worker sends it later. Add a list page with owner names. Show access denial, validation failure, concurrent completion, provider timeout, and a bounded query count.

Write a two-minute explanation: what enters, what rule holds, which writes commit together, what can repeat, and how you verified it. Keep a bug diary with symptom → cause → smallest fix → regression test.

sections.title: What can go wrong
sections.content:
# What can go wrong

A broad rescue in a controller can hide a service failure as a 200. A mocked model can make a callback-heavy feature look simpler than it is. Read the callback registrations and SQL behavior before judging coverage.

**Memory cue:** Trace one path. Break one promise. Prove one repair.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.content:
## Understand the idea

A service object is ordinary Ruby. It earns its place by naming one use case and making its boundary clear. It does not automatically supply permissions, a transaction, retries, or thread safety.

Choose a result contract. A business rejection such as “already closed” can be an expected result. An unexpected database or programmer error should remain visible to monitoring. Do not rescue everything into nil; callers then cannot tell rejection from failure.

State who owns the transaction and which side effects happen later. Keep request-specific data in arguments and local values. Class-level mutable state can leak across calls or threads.

sections.title: Follow a concrete example
sections.content:
## Follow a concrete example

```ruby
# Portable Ruby / Rails 4.2-style service seam.
Result = Struct.new(:ok, :value, :error)
class AssignTicket
  def call(actor:, ticket:, assignee:)
    return Result.new(false, nil, :not_allowed) unless allowed?(actor, ticket)
    Ticket.transaction do
      ticket.update!(assignee_id: assignee.id)
      Result.new(true, ticket.id, nil)
    end
  end
  # allowed? must implement the actual policy; not client-supplied trust.
end
```

sections.title: Trace the execution
sections.content:
## Trace the execution

Controller validates permitted input and identifies actor → service checks the use-case rule → transaction writes → result maps to HTTP. A job caller uses the same rule with a deliberate actor/system role.

Unit-test expected branches with a narrow seam. Use database tests for rollback and constraints. Test the caller’s mapping so a failure is not shown as a success response.

sections.title: Break it and reason about the repair
sections.content:
## Break it and reason about the repair

A service that catches StandardError and returns success hides operational defects. Passing a model from a controller does not mean it belongs to the actor’s tenant.

**Remember:** A service name is not a guarantee. Write the contract.
