  C -->|Yes| T["Try a changed case without notes"]

reading.title: 05 archaeology bisect worktree and advanced tools
reading.content:
# 05 - Archaeology, Bisect, Worktree, And Advanced Tools

Senior Git often means answering hard questions: when did this break, why did this line change, how do I test another branch without losing my state, and how do I repair history without making things worse?

---

## Commit Archaeology

### `git log`

Useful forms:

```bash
git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all
git log --stat
git log -p
git log -- path/to/file
git log --follow -- path/to/file
```

Use `--follow` for a single file when you want Git to follow rename detection across history.

Search commit messages:

```bash
git log --grep='retry'
```

Search added or removed text:

```bash
git log -S 'function_name'
```

Search by regex in patches:

```bash
git log -G 'timeout.*retry'
```

Senior distinction:

- `-S` asks when the count of a string changed
- `-G` asks when a patch line matched a regex

---

## `git show`

Inspect one object:

```bash
git show <commit>
git show <commit>:path/to/file
git show HEAD~2
git show origin/main:README.md
```

Use this to view old file content without switching branches.

---

## `git blame`

Basic:

```bash
git blame path/to/file
```

Ignore whitespace:

```bash
git blame -w path/to/file
```

Limit lines:

```bash
git blame -L 20,80 path/to/file
```

Blame is not for assigning fault. It is for finding context.

Senior workflow:

```bash
git blame -L 40,70 app/service.rb
git show <commit-id>
git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all --ancestry-path <commit-id>..HEAD
```

Then read the PR or surrounding commits if available.

---

## Pickaxe Debugging

Find when a symbol appeared or disappeared:

```bash
git log -S 'calculate_total' -- path/to/file
```

Find commits whose patch matches a pattern:

```bash
git log -G 'calculate_.*total' -- app/
```

Show matching patch:

```bash
git log -p -S 'calculate_total'
```

This is excellent for refactors where the file moved or the obvious blame line is not enough.

---

## Bisect

`git bisect` performs binary search over history.

Start:

```bash
git bisect start
git bisect bad
git bisect good <known-good-commit>
```

Git checks out a midpoint. You test.

```bash
git bisect good
# or
git bisect bad
```

When done:

```bash
git bisect reset
```

Automated:

```bash
git bisect start
git bisect bad
git bisect good <known-good-commit>
git bisect run ./script/test-regression.sh
git bisect reset
```

Test script contract:

```text
exit 0   -> good
exit 1   -> bad
exit 125 -> skip this commit
```

Senior bisect tips:

- First reproduce the bug on current HEAD.
- Pick a known good commit that can run the same test.
- Make the test deterministic.
- If dependencies changed, script the setup or choose a narrower range.
- Use `git bisect skip` for commits that cannot be tested.

---

## Worktree

`git worktree` lets one repository have multiple working directories.

Use cases:

- test another branch without stashing
- run two long builds at once
- hotfix from main while feature work is dirty
- inspect old release code side-by-side

Create:

```bash
git worktree add ../repo-hotfix main
```

Create new branch in a worktree:

```bash
git worktree add -b hotfix/login-timeout ../repo-hotfix origin/main
```

List:

```bash
git worktree list
```

Remove:

```bash
git worktree remove ../repo-hotfix
```

Prune stale metadata:

```bash
git worktree prune
```

Senior intuition: worktree is cleaner than stash when the interruption may last more than a few minutes.

---

## Rerere

`rerere` means reuse recorded resolution.

Enable:

```bash
git config rerere.enabled true
```

When you resolve the same conflict shape again, Git can reuse your previous resolution.

Useful when:

- long-running branch repeatedly rebases on main
- repeated backports hit the same conflict
- release branches carry recurring divergence

Senior caution: still review the resolved result. Reused conflict resolution can be syntactically correct but semantically stale.

---

## Notes

Git notes attach metadata to objects without changing the object id.

```bash
git notes add -m 'Investigated during incident 142'
git notes show
git log --show-notes
```

They are not part of normal branch history. Sharing notes requires fetching/pushing notes refs explicitly.

Use notes for local or team-specific annotations when rewriting commits would be wrong.

---

## Reflog For Branch Movement Analysis

Show branch reflog:

```bash
git reflog show main
git reflog show feature/my-work
```

Show date-based selector:

```bash
git show HEAD@{yesterday}
git diff HEAD@{2.hours.ago}..HEAD
```

This is useful when the question is "what changed in my local branch this afternoon?"

---

## `git fsck`

Find dangling objects:

```bash
git fsck --lost-found
```

This is a deeper recovery tool after refs and reflogs are not enough.

Most daily recovery should start with `git reflog`, not `fsck`.

---

## Packfiles And Maintenance

Git initially writes loose objects. Later it packs them efficiently.

Maintenance commands:

```bash
git gc
git maintenance run
git count-objects -vH
```

Usually Git runs maintenance automatically. Manual use is rare unless a repository is huge or degraded.

Senior intuition: performance problems in Git repos often come from huge binary history, excessive refs, enormous working trees, or pathological file counts.

---

## Sparse Checkout

Sparse checkout lets you populate only part of the working tree.

```bash
git sparse-checkout init --cone
git sparse-checkout set services/api packages/shared
```

Useful in large monorepos.

Trade-off: some tooling assumes the full tree exists. Validate build and editor behavior before adopting it widely.

---

## Partial Clone

Partial clone can avoid downloading every blob immediately.

```bash
git clone --filter=blob:none <url>
```

Git downloads blobs on demand.

Useful for very large repositories. It depends on server support and can shift cost to later operations.

---

## Attributes

`.gitattributes` controls path-specific behavior.

Examples:

```gitattributes
*.sh text eol=lf
*.png binary
docs/** linguist-generated=false
```

Common uses:

- normalize line endings
- mark binary files
- configure custom merge drivers
- improve GitHub language stats

Senior warning: line-ending churn creates noisy diffs and painful blame. Decide normalization early.

---

## Hooks

Hooks are scripts under `.git/hooks`.

Common hooks:

```text
pre-commit
commit-msg
pre-push
post-checkout
```

Local hooks are not versioned by default. Teams often use tools to install shared hooks.

Good hook uses:

- prevent secrets
- run fast format checks
- validate commit messages
- block obvious generated-file mistakes

Bad hook uses:

- slow full test suites on every commit
- hidden behavior that developers cannot reproduce in CI
- policy that exists only locally

Senior rule: hooks are guardrails, not a substitute for CI.

---

## Advanced Inspection Aliases

These aliases are worth having somewhere in your shell or Git config, but understand them before relying on them.

```bash
git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all
git diff --check
git diff --name-status origin/main...HEAD
git log --left-right --cherry-pick --oneline main...feature
```

`--cherry-pick` helps identify equivalent patches even if commit ids differ.

Useful after rebases or cherry-picks:

```bash
git log --left-right --cherry-pick --oneline origin/main...HEAD
```

---

## Senior Debugging Playbooks

### Find when a regression started

```bash
git bisect start
git bisect bad
git bisect good <known-good>
git bisect run ./test-regression.sh
git bisect reset
```

### Understand why a line exists

```bash
git blame -L <start>,<end> path/to/file
git show <commit>
git log -S 'important_string' -- path/to/file
```

### Test a hotfix without touching current work

```bash
git fetch origin
git worktree add -b hotfix/name ../repo-hotfix origin/main
cd ../repo-hotfix
```

### Rescue after a bad rebase

```bash
git reflog
git branch rescue/before-bad-rebase <old-tip>
git reset --hard <old-tip>
```

### Compare patch-equivalent branches

```bash
git log --left-right --cherry-pick --oneline old-branch...new-branch
```

If output is empty, the branches may differ in commit ids but contain equivalent patches.

reading.title: 01 practice labs
reading.content:
# 01 - Git Practice Labs

Use a scratch directory. Do not run these inside an important repository unless the lab explicitly says it is inspection-only.

Recommended setup:

```bash
mkdir -p /tmp/git-mastery-labs
cd /tmp/git-mastery-labs
```

Answers are in `01-practice-labs-answers.md`.

---

## Lab 1: See The Three Trees

Goal: prove that `HEAD`, index, and working tree can hold different versions of the same file.

Tasks:

1. Create a repo.
2. Commit `file.txt` containing `one`.
3. Change it to `two` and stage it.
4. Change it again to `three` without staging.
5. Show:
   - unstaged diff
   - staged diff
   - committed version
   - staged version
   - working tree version

Questions:

- Which version would `git commit` store?
- Which command shows `two -> three`?
- Which command shows `one -> two`?

---

## Lab 2: Write And Inspect Git Objects

Goal: understand blob, tree, and commit objects.

Tasks:

1. Create a repo.
2. Create `note.txt`.
3. Use `git hash-object` before staging.
4. Write the blob object.
5. Stage the file.
6. Use `git write-tree`.
7. Commit.
8. Inspect the commit, tree, and blob with `git cat-file`.

Questions:

- Does the blob know the filename?
- Where is the filename stored?
- What does the commit point to?

---

## Lab 3: Partial Staging

Goal: create one file with two logical edits and commit only one.

Tasks:

1. Create and commit `app.txt` with three lines.
2. Edit line 1 and line 3.
3. Stage only the line 1 change.
4. Commit it.
5. Confirm line 3 is still uncommitted.

Questions:

- Which command lets you stage part of a file?
- Which diff proves the staged patch?
- Which diff proves the unstaged patch?

---

## Lab 4: Two-Dot vs Three-Dot Diff

Goal: see endpoint diff vs branch contribution diff.

Tasks:

1. Create `main` with commits `A` and `B`.
2. Branch `feature` from `B`.
3. Add commit `D` on `feature`.
4. Switch back to `main` and add commit `C`.
5. Compare:
   - `git diff main..feature`
   - `git diff main...feature`
   - `git log main..feature`
   - `git log main...feature`

Questions:

- Which diff resembles a PR diff?
- Why can the two diffs differ?

---

## Lab 5: Merge Conflict

Goal: resolve a real three-way merge conflict.

Tasks:

1. Create a file with `color=blue`.
2. Branch `feature`.
3. On `feature`, change it to `color=green`.
4. On `main`, change it to `color=red`.
5. Merge `feature` into `main`.
6. Resolve final value as `color=purple`.
7. Complete the merge.

Questions:

- What is the merge base?
- What is ours?
- What is theirs?
- Why did Git need help?

---

## Lab 6: Rebase Conflict

Goal: understand conflict flow during rebase.

Tasks:

1. Build the same conflict shape as Lab 5.
2. Instead of merging, rebase `feature` onto `main`.
3. Resolve final value as `color=purple`.
4. Continue the rebase.

Questions:

- Did Git create a merge commit?
- Did the feature commit id change?
- Why can "ours" and "theirs" feel confusing during rebase?

---

## Lab 7: Reset Modes

Goal: compare `--soft`, mixed, and `--hard`.

Tasks:

1. Create three commits: `A`, `B`, `C`.
2. Create a rescue branch.
3. Run `git reset --soft HEAD~1`.
4. Inspect status and log.
5. Return to rescue branch state.
6. Run mixed reset.
7. Inspect status and log.
8. Return to rescue branch state.
9. Run hard reset.
10. Inspect status and log.

Questions:

- Which mode keeps changes staged?
- Which mode keeps changes unstaged?
- Which mode discards file changes?

---

## Lab 8: Recover A Lost Commit

Goal: use reflog as local time travel.

Tasks:

1. Create commits `A`, `B`, `C`.
2. Save the id of `C`.
3. Run `git reset --hard HEAD~2`.
4. Confirm `C` is gone from normal log.
5. Find `C` in the reflog.
6. Recover it with a new branch.

Questions:

- Was commit `C` deleted immediately?
- Which command made it reachable again?

---

## Lab 9: Revert Public History

Goal: undo a commit without rewriting history.

Tasks:

1. Create commits `A`, `B`, `C`.
2. Revert `C`.
3. Inspect log.
4. Inspect file content.

Questions:

- Why is revert safer than reset on shared branches?
- What does the revert commit contain?

---

## Lab 10: Cherry-Pick A Hotfix

Goal: move one fix commit to a release branch.

Tasks:

1. Create `main` with `A`, `B`.
2. Create `release/1.0` from `A`.
3. On `main`, add feature commit `C`.
4. On `main`, add bugfix commit `D`.
5. Cherry-pick only `D` onto `release/1.0`.

Questions:

- Did release receive `C`?
- Did the cherry-picked commit keep the same id?

---

## Lab 11: Bisect A Regression

Goal: find the commit that introduced a failing behavior.

Tasks:

1. Create a small shell script `check.sh` that fails when `app.txt` contains `broken`.
2. Create several commits where one changes `app.txt` to `broken`.
3. Run `git bisect`.
4. Use `git bisect run ./check.sh`.
5. Reset bisect.

Questions:

- What exit code means good?
- What exit code means bad?
- Why is automation better than manual testing here?

---

## Lab 12: Worktree Hotfix

Goal: handle an urgent fix without disturbing dirty feature work.

Tasks:

1. Create a repo with `main`.
2. Create `feature/dirty-work`.
3. Modify files but do not commit.
4. Add a worktree from `main` into a sibling directory.
5. Create a hotfix branch in that worktree.
6. Commit a hotfix there.
7. Return to the original working tree and confirm dirty work is untouched.

Questions:

- Why is worktree better than stash for this case?
- What command lists active worktrees?

---

## Lab 13: Force-With-Lease Reasoning

Goal: understand why `--force-with-lease` exists.

Tasks:

1. Create a bare repo to act as remote.
2. Clone it twice as `alice` and `bob`.
3. Alice pushes a feature branch.
4. Bob fetches and pushes another commit to the same feature branch.
5. Alice rewrites her local feature branch.
6. Alice tries normal push.
7. Alice tries `--force-with-lease`.
8. Alice fetches, inspects, then decides how to integrate.

Questions:

- Why should Alice's force-with-lease fail before fetching?
- What remote work was protected?

---

## Lab 14: Find Why A Line Changed

Goal: combine blame, show, and pickaxe.

Tasks:

1. Create a file with a function or config value.
2. Change it across several commits.
3. Use `git blame` on the final file.
4. Use `git show` on the blamed commit.
5. Use `git log -S` to find when a string was added or removed.

Questions:

- What did blame tell you?
- What did pickaxe tell you that blame did not?

---

## Lab 15: Clean PR Preparation

Goal: turn messy local commits into a reviewable branch.

Tasks:

1. Create a branch from `main`.
2. Make three commits:
   - real feature commit
   - typo fix for the feature
   - unrelated debug change
3. Use `git commit --fixup` or interactive rebase to squash the typo fix.
4. Drop the debug change.
5. Show the final branch contribution.

Questions:

- Which commands show commits unique to your branch?
- Which command shows the PR-style diff?
- Why is this cleanup acceptable before push but risky after others depend on the branch?

trace.title: Known good and bad
trace.detail: Use history tools to answer a question, not to assign blame. log finds commits, show reads a patch, and blame points to the last change for a line. That line may have moved during a refactor, so inspect context.

trace.title: Follow the middle steps
trace.detail:
For eight ordered candidate changes, binary search can often narrow the culprit with only a few checks. The exact sequence follows commit ancestry, not wall-clock guesses.

If the first bad commit is a dependency update, that identifies a trigger, not the whole root cause. Reproduce the behavior and explain why the change activates it. Keep the regression test after the investigation.

trace.title: Check the result
trace.detail: A bisect script with reversed exit meanings gives a confident wrong result. Cleaning a worktree by deleting directories manually can leave registration behind; use git worktree remove for a clean managed checkout after saving needed files.

modules.recallPrompt: Without notes: Use evidence to locate a bad change while keeping active work intact. Give a concrete failure example.

questions.prompt: What must be true for a useful bisect result?
options: The test must reliably distinguish good and bad
The branch must have no merge commits
Every commit message must mention the bug
questions.explanation: Bisect depends on the correctness and repeatability of its classification check.

questions.prompt: Does blame prove the last author caused the bug?
questions.explanation: It identifies a line’s last recorded change. Root cause needs behavioral evidence.

modules.title: Cherry-pick, revert, and moving a fix deliberately
modules.outcome: Move a small fix between release lines and distinguish patch replay from history preservation.
modules.useCase: Backports and shared-history repairs.
modules.benefits: Small fixes can move without unrelated features.
modules.drawbacks: Dependencies and merge semantics can make a small patch nontrivial.
modules.version: Modern Git; check git --version for command availability
modules.cue: Move the patch. Check its assumptions.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.content:
## Understand the idea

Cherry-pick applies a commit’s change onto the current base and usually creates a new commit. It does not bring every dependency of that change automatically. A patch that applies cleanly can still call a helper absent on the release branch.

Revert creates a new corrective commit. It is often easier for collaborators than rewriting a published branch. Reverting a merge requires choosing the intended mainline parent and understanding future merge consequences; do not guess from parent numbers.

Before any history operation, inspect the graph, outgoing patch, and current work. Use a disposable worktree for a release rehearsal. Record which release line received the fix and how it was tested there.

sections.title: Follow a concrete example
sections.content:
## Follow a concrete example

```sh
git show <fix-id> --stat
git show <fix-id>
# In a clean, deliberate release-fix branch/worktree:
git cherry-pick <fix-id>
# On conflict, inspect intent, then continue or abort:
git cherry-pick --abort
```

Replace placeholders with inspected IDs. Do not execute these commands in an unrelated active checkout.

sections.title: Trace the execution
sections.content:
## Trace the execution

Fix on main → inspect dependencies → replay onto release branch → resolve intent → test release configuration → review. The new commit ID can differ even when the patch is similar.

For a revert, test the resulting behavior with later changes present. A reverse patch is not a reversal of every external effect or migration.

sections.title: Break it and reason about the repair
sections.content:
## Break it and reason about the repair

A clean cherry-pick can be behaviorally incomplete. Reverting a migration commit does not reconstruct deleted data. Shared branch rewrites need coordination.

**Remember:** Move the patch. Check its assumptions.

exercises.title: Diagnose and repair
exercises.prompt:
## Diagnose and repair

A hotfix cherry-picks cleanly but fails because a helper was introduced in an earlier main commit. Repair the release plan.

Before opening a reference, write your prediction, the exact change, how you would verify it, and why it works. Use synthetic data and a separate lab. State clearly which checks you actually ran.
exercises.solution:
## One valid repair

Identify the minimal dependency or adapt the fix to the older contract. Test the actual release branch in a clean worktree. Avoid dragging a large unrelated feature into the release just to obtain a helper.

A different answer can work if it meets the stated rule. Explain the failure timeline and the tradeoff. A product name or a longer answer is not proof.

exercises.title: Change the situation
exercises.prompt:
## Change the situation

A bad merge is already shared. What must be inspected before reverting it?

Before opening a reference, write your prediction, the exact change, how you would verify it, and why it works. Use synthetic data and a separate lab. State clearly which checks you actually ran.
exercises.solution:
## One valid transfer

Inspect both parents, the intended mainline, later dependent changes, and the resulting behavior. Explain how the revert affects future merges. Preserve shared ancestry and test the corrective patch.

A different answer can work if it meets the stated rule. Explain the failure timeline and the tradeoff. A product name or a longer answer is not proof.

modules.title: Conflicts are behavior decisions
modules.outcome: Resolve a conflict by comparing base and both intents, then test the combined rule.
modules.useCase: Refactors overlapping feature and access changes.
modules.benefits: Preserves meaning rather than merely producing parseable text.
modules.drawbacks: The correct answer may require a product/API decision.
modules.version: Modern Git; check git --version for command availability

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.content:
## Understand the idea

Conflict markers identify text Git could not combine automatically. They do not tell you which product behavior should win. Read the common base, each change, callers, and tests.

During rebase, Git replays your commits onto another base. The meanings of ours and theirs can feel reversed from an ordinary merge. Inspect actual content rather than clicking a side label by habit.

Some dangerous conflicts are semantic and have no markers: one change renames a field while another still sends the old field; one adds a new state while another assumes only two states. Test the combined contract even after a clean merge.

sections.title: Follow a concrete example
sections.content:
## Follow a concrete example

```sh
git status
git diff
git show :1:path/to/file  # common base, when present in an unmerged index
git show :2:path/to/file  # one side
git show :3:path/to/file  # other side
```

In a scratch repository, make one branch add authorization and another refactor the method. The final code must preserve both the new structure and the permission rule.

sections.title: Trace the execution
sections.content:
## Trace the execution

Write intended before/after behavior for each branch. Decide the combined behavior. Edit the resolution, stage it, continue the operation, and run the relevant regression tests. If the operation is wrong for the task, abort deliberately after preserving needed work.

Use the graph to explain where the resolution lives. A merge commit can contain meaningful hand-written conflict decisions that deserve review.

sections.title: Break it and reason about the repair
sections.content:
## Break it and reason about the repair

Accept Both can duplicate work or create unreachable code. Accept Current can remove a new rule. Conflict-free text can still be an invalid combined design.

**Remember:** Keep both intentions when both are still valid.

exercises.title: Diagnose and repair
exercises.prompt:
## Diagnose and repair

A conflict resolution keeps a refactor but drops a newly added access check. Write a repair and regression test plan.

Before opening a reference, write your prediction, the exact change, how you would verify it, and why it works. Use synthetic data and a separate lab. State clearly which checks you actually ran.
exercises.solution:
## One valid repair

Recover both intended changes from the base/sides, restore the access rule in the refactored path, and test allowed/denied cases. Review the resolved patch rather than only checking that markers disappeared.

A different answer can work if it meets the stated rule. Explain the failure timeline and the tradeoff. A product name or a longer answer is not proof.

exercises.title: Change the situation
exercises.prompt:
## Change the situation

A clean merge changes an API field name on one side but not its caller. How would you catch it?

Before opening a reference, write your prediction, the exact change, how you would verify it, and why it works. Use synthetic data and a separate lab. State clearly which checks you actually ran.
exercises.solution:
## One valid transfer

Run a contract/integration check for the connected caller and endpoint. Search call sites and inspect both changes’ intent. Textual success is not API compatibility.

A different answer can work if it meets the stated rule. Explain the failure timeline and the tradeoff. A product name or a longer answer is not proof.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.content:
## Understand the idea

Use reflog to find a recent local reference movement, then name the candidate commit with a rescue branch before changing anything else. Reflog is local and expires; it does not store every unsaved file.

Use bisect only after a repeatable good/bad check exists. A flaky network dependency can make a confident wrong culprit. Verify the check against known endpoints of the search.

A worktree gives a separate checkout for the exact committed snapshot. It helps avoid accidentally testing a staged patch together with unstaged helper changes. Save needed files before removing a worktree, and use Git’s worktree commands to keep registration consistent.

sections.title: Follow a concrete example
sections.content:
## Follow a concrete example

```sh
git reflog -10
git show <candidate-id> --stat
git branch rescue/investigation <candidate-id>
git worktree add --detach ../ticket-investigation <candidate-id>
# Run the repeatable test there, then inspect its result.
git worktree list
```

Use a fresh scratch location. A detached worktree is suitable for inspection; create a deliberate branch if you intend to keep new commits.

sections.title: Trace the execution
sections.content:
## Trace the execution

Observed regression → minimal deterministic check → known-good/bad commits → bisect or exact-snapshot comparison → inspect trigger → preserve regression test. Keep the active worktree’s edits untouched.

A first-bad dependency update is a trigger to investigate, not automatically the root explanation. Reproduce the mechanism after locating the change.

sections.title: Break it and reason about the repair
sections.content:
## Break it and reason about the repair

A test can fail because its historical build environment is unavailable. Mark such commits untestable/skip rather than bad. A cleanup command can delete untracked work that Git never stored.

**Remember:** Preserve work. Reproduce the symptom. Search the graph.

modules.outcome: Review a change, integrate upstream work, and preserve a traceable release without rewriting shared history casually.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.content:
## Understand the idea

Before review, compare against the intended base and inspect the actual outgoing patch. Explain the trigger, resulting behavior, test evidence, and known limitation. A long commit list is not a substitute for that explanation.

Fetch updates your remote-tracking knowledge. Integration is a separate decision. A rejected push means the remote state changed; inspect before deciding how to integrate. force-with-lease is a check against an expected tip, not permission to surprise collaborators.

For a release, name the exact commit/artifact, schema compatibility assumptions, and rollback/data-recovery plan. Keep hotfix backports traceable. A Git tag names a version but does not prove the deployed container matches it; connect it to an image digest or build record.

sections.title: Follow a concrete example
sections.content:
## Follow a concrete example

```sh
git fetch origin
git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD
git diff --stat origin/main...HEAD
git diff origin/main...HEAD
git status --short
```

Do not publish, tag a shared release, or rewrite shared branches as an automatic course exercise. Practice the graph in a disposable local remote.

sections.title: Trace the execution
sections.content:
## Trace the execution

Reviewable branch → fetch and compare → relevant tests → reviewed integration → immutable build identity → release observation. Keep the relation between source revision and deployed artifact visible.

Use small commits that can be understood and, when necessary, reverted meaningfully. Separate a mechanical rename from a behavior change when that improves review.

**Remember:** Review the patch. Release the artifact. Keep the link.

modules.title: From URL to pixels
modules.outcome: Trace navigation, browser work, and the boundary between server and client.

modules.version: Portable JavaScript · React hooks · Vue 2/3 comparisons · Next App Router

sections.title: The idea
sections.content:
# The idea

The browser turns a URL into a request, receives HTML, builds a DOM tree, loads CSS and JavaScript, and paints pixels. JavaScript can change the DOM later. Layout calculates geometry. Paint draws visible styles. These are different costs.

In a client-routed app, clicking a link may update browser history and UI without requesting a whole new document. Refreshing that URL is still a server request, so the server needs an appropriate route fallback. A blank page after refresh can be a serving/configuration bug rather than a component bug.

HTML from server rendering can appear before client JavaScript is interactive. Hydration connects client behavior to that initial markup. Initial client output must agree with the server output where hydration expects a match.

sections.title: A small example
Follow the execution
sections.content:
# Follow the execution

Trace document request → HTML parsing → CSS/layout → script → UI change. Then trace a client navigation separately. The network requests and work can differ.

For a slow page, determine whether the wait is server response time, asset loading, script execution, layout, or a later API call. A single “loading” label hides several possible causes.

sections.title: What can go wrong
sections.content:
# What can go wrong

A new Date() or random value rendered independently on server and client can produce different first markup. Browser-only APIs such as localStorage are not available during server execution.

**Memory cue:** URL → request → tree → layout → paint.

Close this lesson. Draw the five steps. Explain one failure in your own words before opening Practice.

exercises.title: Find and fix the bug
exercises.prompt:
# Find and fix the bug

A client route works after clicking but returns a server 404 on refresh. Explain the missing boundary.

Write: prediction → proposed change → observed evidence → explanation. Run code only in a separate training sandbox. If you did not run it, say so. Submit before opening a reference.
exercises.solution:
# One valid repair

Refresh asks the server for that path as a document. Configure the deployment to serve the SPA shell for valid client routes while preserving real asset/API 404 behavior. Test direct navigation, refresh, and back/forward.

**How to check:** Application code or a router must react to that history change and render the view.

Other repairs are acceptable if they satisfy the stated rule. Explain the failure timeline and show a relevant test. Code length and matching keywords are not evidence.

Use a stable server-provided initial value, or a deliberate placeholder that matches on both sides before starting client updates. Do not assume suppressing a warning fixes a real data mismatch.

**Explain back:** URL → request → tree → layout → paint. What changed in the new condition? What would make your answer fail?

reading.title: 00 spa mental model and browser internals
reading.content:
# 00 - SPA Mental Model And Browser Internals This doc is the foundation. React, Next, and Vue sit on top of the browser. If the browser model is weak, framework behavior feels magical. If the browser model is strong, most frontend decisions become mechanical. --- ## The Core Idea A Single Page Application is not a page that never reloads. It is an application that takes responsibility for work the browser used to do by default: ```text traditional page browser requests URL server returns HTML browser displays a full document navigation asks the server for a new document SPA browser loads an app shell JavaScript owns routing, state, rendering, and interaction navigation often changes UI without replacing the full document ``` That shift gives you smoother interactions, richer state, and less full-page interruption. It also gives you more ways to break loading, routing, accessibility, caching, performance, and back-button behavior. Senior intuition: a SPA borrows power from the browser, but also borrows responsibility. --- ## The Frontend Loop Every interactive screen repeatedly does this: ```text input user clicks, types, scrolls, drags, focuses, navigates event browser dispatches an event to JavaScript state transition code decides what changed render calculation framework computes the next UI description commit framework mutates the DOM browser rendering style -> layout -> paint -> composite feedback user sees, hears, or feels the result ``` When a UI feels bad, ask which link in this loop failed. Examples: - Click feels dead -> missing immediate feedback or blocked main thread. - Page jumps -> layout changed after paint without reserved space. - Spinner flashes -> loading state is technically correct but emotionally noisy. - Back button breaks -> router state and URL state disagree. - Form loses input -> component identity changed and local state was destroyed. --- ## Browser Loading Pipeline When the browser receives a document, it builds several internal structures: ```text HTML bytes -> tokens -> DOM tree CSS bytes -> CSSOM tree DOM + CSSOM -> render tree -> layout boxes -> paint commands -> compositor layers -> pixels ``` JavaScript can interrupt this pipeline because scripts may read or mutate the document. Example: ```html
``` The browser cannot pretend the script has no effect. It must run it at the right time. Senior intuition: HTML and CSS are streaming-friendly. JavaScript is often a checkpoint. --- ## Critical Rendering Path The browser wants to show useful pixels quickly. The critical path is the minimum work needed before first meaningful display: ```text HTML needed for structure CSS needed for visible styling font choices that affect text display JavaScript that blocks rendering or hydration images needed above the fold ``` Bad version: ```text HTML arrives -> giant CSS blocks render -> giant JS downloads -> JS parses -> JS executes -> app fetches data -> app renders -> user finally sees useful UI ``` Better version: ```text HTML arrives with useful shell or content -> critical CSS is small -> non-critical JS is delayed or split -> layout space is reserved -> user sees stable progress -> interactivity arrives progressively ``` Interesting fact: a page can have fast network timing and still feel slow if the first visible thing is blank, unstable, or unresponsive. --- ## The Main Thread Most frontend JavaScript runs on the main thread. The main thread also handles many browser tasks: ```text parse HTML run JavaScript calculate styles layout paint setup dispatch events run timers run promise callbacks ``` If your JavaScript runs too long, the browser cannot respond. Example: ```js button.addEventListener('click', () => { const startedAt = performance.now(); while (performance.now() - startedAt < 300) { // Simulate expensive work. } button.textContent = 'Done'; }); ``` The user clicked immediately, but the visual response waits until the task ends. Senior intuition: a blocked main thread is not "slow JavaScript" only. It is delayed input, delayed paint, delayed feedback, and lost trust. --- ## Event Loop In Frontend Terms The event loop coordinates work: ```text take one task -> run JavaScript until the stack is empty -> run queued microtasks -> browser may render -> take next task ``` Common task sources: ```text tasks click event, timer callback, network event, script execution microtasks promise callbacks, queueMicrotask, mutation observer callbacks render opportunity style, layout, paint, composite ``` Example: ```js console.log('A'); setTimeout(() => { console.log('B'); }, 0); Promise.resolve().then(() => { console.log('C'); }); console.log('D'); ``` Output: ```text A D C B ``` Why: ```text current script task runs first promise microtask runs before next task timer task runs later ``` Senior intuition: promises do not make code parallel. They schedule continuations. --- ## Layout, Paint, Composite Browser rendering is not one operation. ```text style Which CSS rules apply? layout What size and position is every box? paint What pixels need to be drawn for borders, text, shadows, backgrounds? composite How are layers combined on screen? ``` Some changes are more expensive than others: ```text change width may trigger layout, paint, composite change color may trigger paint, composite change transform often only composite change opacity often only composite ``` This is why animations usually prefer: ```css .panel { transform: translateY(0); opacity: 1; } ``` over: ```css .panel { top: 0; height: 300px; } ``` Do not memorize property lists. Memorize the question: ```text Did I change geometry, pixels, or only layer composition? ``` --- ## Forced Layout The browser batches layout work when possible. You can accidentally force it to stop and calculate layout immediately: ```js box.style.width = '300px'; const width = box.offsetWidth; box.style.height = `${width / 2}px`; ``` Reading `offsetWidth` after writing layout-affecting styles forces the browser to answer "what is the layout now?" Bad loop: ```js items.forEach((item) => { item.style.width = '300px'; const height = item.offsetHeight; item.style.marginTop = `${height / 4}px`; }); ``` Better shape: ```js const itemHeights = items.map((item) => item.offsetHeight); items.forEach((item, index) => { item.style.width = '300px'; item.style.marginTop = `${itemHeights[index] / 4}px`; }); ``` Senior intuition: separate reads from writes when touching layout directly. --- ## SPA Routing Classic navigation: ```text click link -> browser requests new HTML document -> previous JavaScript context disappears ``` SPA navigation: ```text click link -> router intercepts navigation -> history API updates URL -> app chooses route component -> app fetches data if needed -> app renders new screen ``` The URL still matters. A good SPA preserves browser expectations: - refresh should keep the same screen when possible - back and forward should behave predictably - links should be real links when navigation is intended - important view state should be shareable when users expect sharing - route changes should announce meaningful context for assistive tech Bad smell: ```text The screen changes, but the URL does not. ``` Sometimes that is fine for a tab inside a card. It is usually wrong for product-level navigation. --- ## Rendering Modes Modern frontend is not only SPA versus server pages. Useful mental model: ```text CSR - client-side rendering Browser gets a shell. JavaScript builds most UI. SSR - server-side rendering Server returns HTML for the current request. JavaScript may hydrate it. SSG - static generation HTML is created ahead of time. ISR or revalidation Static output updates on a schedule or trigger. Streaming Server sends UI in chunks as data becomes ready. Partial hydration or islands Only some regions become interactive. ``` Trade-off map: ```text Need fast first content? Prefer server or static HTML. Need rich authenticated app behavior? Client rendering may be fine after login. Need SEO or share previews? Server or static output helps. Need highly personalized data? Think carefully about caching and server/client boundaries. Need instant local interaction? Keep that interaction close to the client. ``` Senior intuition: rendering is data placement plus interaction placement. --- ## Hydration Hydration means: ```text server sends HTML browser displays it JavaScript loads framework attaches event handlers and internal state to existing DOM ``` Hydration can fail or feel bad when: - server HTML does not match client render - client needs data the server did not have - too much JavaScript must load before interaction - the page looks ready but ignores clicks - browser extensions or time-dependent values alter markup Example mismatch: ```js function Clock() { return

{new Date().toLocaleTimeString()}

; } ``` The server time and client time may differ. Better shape: ```js function Clock() { const [time, setTime] = useState(null); useEffect(() => { setTime(new Date().toLocaleTimeString()); }, []); return

{time || 'Loading time...'}

; } ``` This makes the unstable value explicitly client-owned. Senior intuition: hydration is not free. It is the cost of turning already-visible HTML into a living app. --- ## What Makes A SPA Feel Fast Not just: ```text low API latency small bundle high Lighthouse score ``` Also: ```text immediate acknowledgement stable layout clear loading shape optimistic feedback where safe short main-thread tasks predictable navigation cached repeated work useful empty states recoverable errors ``` Example: ```text User clicks Save. Bad: Button does nothing for 800ms, then changes. Better: Button immediately shows "Saving..." duplicate clicks are prevented form remains stable success appears near the action failure gives recovery ``` Fast is a feeling created by technical and interaction design choices together. --- ## Senior Debugging Questions When a frontend issue is vague, ask: - Is this a loading problem, interaction problem, rendering problem, data problem, or perception problem? - Is the main thread blocked? - Did the browser paint before the expensive work? - Is layout shifting because space was not reserved? - Is state duplicated between URL, cache, component, and form? - Is the user waiting without knowing the system heard them? - Is this broken only before hydration, after hydration, or after navigation? - Did we optimize the wrong phase of the experience? --- ## The One-Sentence Model A SPA is an event-driven state machine running inside the browser rendering pipeline. If you know the state machine and the pipeline, you can reason about almost anything.

reading.title: 01 js engine and runtime
reading.content:
# 01 - The JavaScript Engine and Runtime

> Why this file matters to you as a senior dev: every framework you use sits on a JS engine and a host runtime. When perf gets weird, hydration mismatches, or async ordering bites, the bug almost always lives at this layer. You want to be able to point at the layer, not guess.

---

## The two things people conflate

The first thing to untangle: "JavaScript engine" and "JavaScript runtime" are different.

The **engine** parses and executes JS. V8 in Chrome and Node, JavaScriptCore in Safari, SpiderMonkey in Firefox. The engine knows about syntax, values, the call stack, the heap, and garbage collection. It does not know about `setTimeout`, `fetch`, or the DOM.

The **runtime** is the engine plus everything around it: the event loop, the task queues, the host APIs (DOM in browsers, `fs` in Node), and the threading model that makes the engine actually do useful work.

> 💡 Insight - when you say "JavaScript is single-threaded", you mean the engine's call stack is single-threaded. The runtime around it is wildly multi-threaded. The browser parses HTML, paints pixels, runs network I/O, and decodes images on other threads. They just don't share the JS heap.

---

## V8 in one diagram

```text
        source code
            |
            v
       [ Parser ]  --produces-->  AST
            |
            v
       [ Ignition ]  -->  bytecode + interpreter
            |
            | (hot code paths flagged)
            v
       [ TurboFan ]  -->  optimized machine code
            |
            | (deopt if assumptions break)
            v
       back to bytecode
```

V8 starts with the interpreter (Ignition) so your code runs fast. As functions get called repeatedly with consistent shapes, TurboFan compiles them down to optimized machine code. If the assumptions break later (a function was always called with `number`, suddenly gets a `string`), V8 deoptimizes back to bytecode.

This is why "tight loops over consistent shapes are fast" is real engineering advice and not folklore.

```js
function sumPoints(points) {
  let total = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < points.length; i++) {
    total += points[i].x + points[i].y;
  }
  return total;
}
```

If every `point` has the same shape (same property order, same types), TurboFan loves this loop. If you sometimes pass `{ x, y }` and sometimes `{ y, x }` or `{ x, y, z }`, V8 keeps churning through different hidden classes and the optimized version doesn't stick.

> ⚠️ Trap - building objects by adding properties in different orders across your code base creates different hidden classes for what looks like "the same shape". For frequently-allocated objects in hot paths, set all properties in the constructor in the same order, every time.

---

## Hidden classes and inline caches

V8 doesn't store objects as hash maps the way the JS spec implies. It builds a **hidden class** (also called a "shape" or "map") that records property names and offsets. Two objects with the same hidden class can be accessed by the same machine-code path.

```js
function makePoint(x, y) {
  const point = {};
  point.x = x;     // hidden class C1
  point.y = y;     // hidden class C2 (transitions from C1)
  return point;
}

function makeWeird(x, y) {
  const point = {};
  point.y = y;     // hidden class C1' (different from C1!)
  point.x = x;     // hidden class C2' (not the same as C2)
  return point;
}
```

Two functions, "same" object, two completely different hidden class chains. The optimizer can't share machine code between them.

**Inline caches** are the next step: when V8 compiles `point.x`, it remembers "for hidden class C2, `x` is at offset 0". Next call with the same shape skips the lookup. Across many shapes, the cache gets polluted ("megamorphic") and access slows down.

> 🔍 Under the Hood - this is why frameworks like Vue, when shipping reactive proxies, are careful about how they wrap objects. Wrapping a reactive object inside another reactive object would cascade hidden-class transitions and tank performance for tight reactive paths.

---

## The call stack and the heap

Two memory regions you should be able to picture:

```text
  Stack                         Heap
+---------+                +-----------------+
| frame 3 |                | { x: 1, y: 2 }  |
+---------+                | "hello"         |
| frame 2 |                | function () {}  |
+---------+                | [1, 2, 3]       |
| frame 1 |                +-----------------+
+---------+
```

Stack holds **frames**: one per function call. Each frame has its local variables and a return address. When the function returns, the frame is popped. This is why deep recursion blows up: you exceed the stack's fixed budget.

Heap holds **objects**: anything that isn't a primitive lives here. Variables on the stack often hold a reference (a pointer) into the heap.

```js
function makeUser() {
  const name = 'Asha';
  const user = { name };  // user lives on the stack as a reference
  return user;            // the object itself stays in the heap
}

const u = makeUser();     // u still points at that heap object
```

`makeUser`'s frame is gone, but the object survives because something still references it. That's the basis of garbage collection.

---

## Garbage collection in two sentences

V8 uses a **generational GC**: most objects die young, so it splits the heap into a "young generation" (cheap to scan, scanned often) and an "old generation" (expensive to scan, scanned rarely). When you allocate, you get a slot in the young space. If you survive a couple of GC cycles, you get promoted to the old space.

The senior takeaway is not "do GC manually". It's **understand what keeps objects alive longer than you think**: closures, arrays you forgot to clear, event listeners you never removed, detached DOM nodes a component still holds a ref to.

```js
function attachLogger(button) {
  const buffer = new Array(1_000_000).fill('log');
  button.addEventListener('click', () => {
    console.log(buffer.length);
  });
}
```

That `buffer` lives forever, even after `attachLogger` returns, because the click handler closes over it. If you never remove the listener, you never free the buffer.

> ⚠️ Trap - DevTools "memory" tab shows you the leak after you have it. The cheaper habit is to assume any subscription, listener, observer, or timer is a leak unless you can name where it gets cleaned up.

---

## The event loop, properly

Here is the model worth memorizing.

```text
+--------------------------------------+
|             Call stack               |
+--------------------------------------+
              ^
              | (run to completion)
              |
+--------------------------------------+
|         Microtask queue              |  <- Promise callbacks, queueMicrotask
+--------------------------------------+
              ^
              | (drain fully between tasks)
              |
+--------------------------------------+
|           Task queue                 |  <- timers, I/O, click events, etc.
+--------------------------------------+
              ^
              | (one task per loop turn)
              |
        [ event loop ]  -- yields to browser rendering opportunities
```

Each tick:

1. Pull one **task** off the task queue. Push its callback onto the stack.
2. Run it to completion. The stack must be empty before we move on.
3. Drain the **entire microtask queue**. Every promise continuation queued during step 2, plus any queued during step 3 itself.
4. The browser may do a render pass.
5. Repeat.

```js
console.log('A');

setTimeout(() => console.log('B'), 0);

Promise.resolve().then(() => {
  console.log('C');
  Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('D'));
});

console.log('E');
```

Output:

```text
A
E
C
D
B
```

`A` and `E` are synchronous. The promise microtasks (`C`, then `D` queued from inside `C`) drain fully before the timer task `B` runs.

> 💡 Insight - a long microtask chain can starve rendering. If you keep queueing promise continuations from inside promise continuations, the browser cannot get a paint in. This is why `await` in a tight loop can feel slow and freeze the UI even when individual awaits look fine.

---

## await is just sugar over microtasks

This is the part that fixes most async confusion.

```js
async function save() {
  setStatus('saving');
  await api.save();
  setStatus('saved');
}
```

Mentally rewrite that as:

```js
function save() {
  setStatus('saving');
  return api.save().then(() => {
    setStatus('saved');
  });
}
```

Everything after an `await` is a microtask continuation. The function does not pause. It returns a promise immediately, and the rest is scheduled.

This is why:

```js
button.addEventListener('click', async () => {
  setLoading(true);
  await fetchData();
  setLoading(false);
});
```

The first `setLoading(true)` runs synchronously inside the click handler. The `setLoading(false)` runs as a microtask after `fetchData` resolves. If another click happens between, you have two in-flight requests racing each other, and the one that resolves last wins. The handler being `async` did not buy you any concurrency safety.

> ⚠️ Trap - `async` functions return immediately. If your event handler is async and you don't track the in-flight request, you're inventing race conditions for free.

---

## Tasks vs microtasks for frameworks

React, Vue, and most async-aware libraries lean hard on the microtask queue.

- React schedules state updates and tries to flush them as microtasks within the same event so multiple `setState` calls coalesce into one render.
- Vue's reactive system schedules re-renders into the microtask queue (`nextTick` is built on this).

That's why:

```js
count.value += 1;
console.log(button.textContent);  // still old value
await nextTick();
console.log(button.textContent);  // updated
```

Vue scheduled the update, but it hasn't flushed yet. Your sync `console.log` ran before the microtask drained.

> 🔍 Under the Hood - `Promise.resolve().then(...)` is the cheapest "do this after the current sync code" primitive. `setTimeout(..., 0)` is *much* slower because it enters the task queue, which means rendering opportunities first.

---

## Memory model and what "shared" means

Workers and the main thread don't share JS heap memory. They communicate via `postMessage`, which copies (or transfers) data. The exception is `SharedArrayBuffer` plus `Atomics`, which gives you actual shared memory but requires cross-origin isolation headers.

This matters because the easy answer to "JS is single-threaded" is "use workers". And it works, but you need to think about serialization cost.

```js
const worker = new Worker('parse.js');

worker.postMessage(hugeBlob);  // hugeBlob is structured-cloned
```

A 50 MB object getting cloned to send to a worker can be slower than just doing the work on the main thread. Transferable objects (`ArrayBuffer`, `MessagePort`, etc.) can be moved instead of copied, which is the senior workaround.

> Interesting fact: Chrome's V8 and Node.js share the same engine, which is why Node feature parity with browser JS is so tight. The runtime around it is completely different (no DOM, but `fs`, `net`, `process`, etc.), but the language and engine are the same binary lineage.

---

## A tiny mental checklist for engine-related debugging

When something feels off at the engine layer, ask in this order:

1. Is this code running on the call stack right now, or has it been queued? If queued, microtask or task?
2. Is this object's shape consistent across the hot path?
3. Is something keeping a reference alive past the lifetime I expected?
4. Am I assuming `await` pauses the world? It doesn't.

Most "weird async" or "weird perf" bugs collapse to one of these.

---

## What to carry forward

- The engine runs JS. The runtime gives it timers, I/O, the DOM, the event loop. They are different layers; debug at the right one.
- V8 optimizes for consistent object shapes and consistent call sites. Inconsistency forces deoptimization.
- The event loop runs one task, fully drains microtasks, then maybe paints. Long microtask chains starve rendering.
- `await` is not a pause. Code after it is a microtask continuation. Race conditions are easy to invent if you forget that.
- Objects survive as long as something references them. Closures, listeners, timers, and detached DOM are the usual suspects when memory grows.

modules.outcome: Distinguish missing, null, false, zero, and shared nested state when adapting API data.
modules.useCase: Support forms with optional flags, numeric limits, and editable tag lists.
modules.benefits: Fewer invisible defaulting and Cancel bugs.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.content:
## Understand the idea

A browser receives values, not intentions. A missing field can mean “leave unchanged.” null can mean “clear it.” false and zero can be valid choices. Decide those meanings in the API contract before choosing a default operator.

Use ?? when the fallback should apply to null or undefined. Use || only when all falsey values should trigger the fallback. Destructuring and spread copy one level. A new outer object may still share nested objects with the original. That can make Cancel accidentally change the saved record.

Treat JSON as outside input. JSON.parse proves that text is valid JSON; it does not prove that the result has a ticket ID, an allowed status, or a sensible array shape. Validate at the boundary, then pass a stable internal shape to components.

sections.title: Follow a concrete example
Trace the execution
sections.content:
## Trace the execution

Trace load → validate → adapt → edit draft → submit → accept server result. Keep server data separate from unsaved edits. Test an absent field, explicit null, false, zero, and an empty string. They are five distinct cases.

If a nested structure is complex, copy the fields the form actually edits rather than cloning an entire model graph. structuredClone supports many values but not functions or every host object; it is not a universal serialization protocol.

sections.title: Break it and reason about the repair
sections.content:
## Break it and reason about the repair

Using value || default can silently change a valid zero. Copying only the outer object can leak draft changes. Parsing valid JSON can still produce the wrong type.

**Remember:** Absence is a contract. Copy only what you own.

modules.title: JavaScript functions, closures, and object lookup
modules.outcome: Predict captured values, call-time this, and property lookup in everyday UI code.
modules.useCase: Event handlers, timers, reusable utilities, and callback APIs.
modules.benefits: Makes callback behavior predictable.
modules.drawbacks: Retained state and implicit receivers can hide ownership.
modules.version: Modern JavaScript / TypeScript · Vue 3.5 where applicable · browser APIs
modules.cue: Creation decides scope. Calling decides normal this.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.content:
## Understand the idea

A function can keep access to variables from the scope where it was created. That is a closure. It captures a binding, not always a frozen copy of the value. A later mutation can change what a callback reads. Each function call can also create a separate binding, which is why a factory can give each widget private state.

For a normal function, this depends on how it is called. obj.method() supplies obj. Taking const fn=obj.method and calling fn() loses that receiver in strict mode. An arrow keeps this from its enclosing scope; it does not acquire a new receiver through obj.arrow().

Objects have their own properties and a prototype chain. A missing own property can still be found on the prototype. Use Object.hasOwn when ownership matters. Prefer Map for arbitrary key/value lookup when object-prototype behavior would be surprising. These rules explain callbacks and objects; you rarely need to build a custom inheritance tree for a Vue page.

sections.title: Follow a concrete example
Trace the execution
sections.content:
## Trace the execution

Trace creation → retained binding → callback invocation. Distinguish the value at registration from the value at execution. Then trace the call expression to find this.

For object lookup, check own properties first, then the prototype chain. Object.create(null) has no usual Object prototype; it also lacks methods such as hasOwnProperty. Object.hasOwn(obj,key) works without calling a method from untrusted input.

sections.title: Break it and reason about the repair
sections.content:
## Break it and reason about the repair

A callback can keep large objects alive after the screen closes. A detached method can lose this. Checking obj[key] alone can confuse absent values with inherited properties or valid falsey values.

**Remember:** Creation decides scope. Calling decides normal this.

modules.title: Closures, tasks, and async races
modules.outcome: Predict JavaScript ordering and prevent old requests from replacing new results.
modules.cue: Start order is not finish order.
modules.version: Portable JavaScript · React hooks · Vue 2/3 comparisons · Next App Router

sections.title: The idea
sections.content:
# The idea

JavaScript code runs on a call stack. Browser events and timers schedule later tasks. Promise callbacks use a microtask queue, which is drained after the current stack before the next task. A zero-delay timer means “eligible later,” not “run now.”

Closures retain access to lexical bindings. const prevents rebinding the name; it does not freeze the object. let in a loop creates useful per-iteration bindings. Prototype lookup chooses inherited properties when an own property is absent.

Async requests can finish out of order. If a search for “ca” finishes after “cat,” blindly applying both results makes the screen go backward. Cancellation can save work, but a latest-request check makes the UI’s acceptance rule explicit.

sections.title: A small example
Follow the execution
sections.content:
# Follow the execution

Write the synchronous lines first: A and D. Then drain the promise callback: C. Then the timer task can run: B.

For search, label each request with a number. Only the latest number may publish rows. Also guard loading/error updates; a stale failure must not replace the current success. Encode user input when putting it into a URL.

sections.title: What can go wrong
sections.content:
# What can go wrong

await pauses that async function, not the whole browser. A long synchronous loop still blocks input. A stale request can also clear the current loading spinner if only result assignment is guarded.

**Memory cue:** Start order is not finish order.

Close this lesson. Draw the five steps. Explain one failure in your own words before opening Practice.

exercises.title: Find and fix the bug
exercises.prompt:
# Find and fix the bug

A typeahead guards rows with a request number but always sets loading=false in finally. Explain the remaining race.

Write: prediction → proposed change → observed evidence → explanation. Run code only in a separate training sandbox. If you did not run it, say so. Submit before opening a reference.
exercises.solution:
# One valid repair

An older request can finish while the newest is pending and hide its spinner. Guard loading/error/finally state with the same latest-request identity. Abort obsolete requests when useful, and test old-success/new-success plus old-error/new-success orderings.

**How to check:** The browser drains queued microtasks before choosing the next task. This does not promise order between unrelated network responses.

Other repairs are acceptable if they satisfy the stated rule. Explain the failure timeline and show a relevant test. Code length and matching keywords are not evidence.

exercises.title: Change one condition
exercises.prompt:
# Change one condition

A component unmounts while a request is pending. What should cleanup do?

Write: prediction → proposed change → observed evidence → explanation. Run code only in a separate training sandbox. If you did not run it, say so. Submit before opening a reference.
exercises.solution:
# One valid adaptation

Cancel work when supported and mark that result as no longer acceptable. Prevent stale state updates and remove listeners/timers. Distinguish an intentional AbortError from an error shown to the user.

**Explain back:** Start order is not finish order. What changed in the new condition? What would make your answer fail?

modules.outcome: Model request states and narrow outside data instead of hiding uncertainty with any.
modules.useCase: API adapters and reusable Vue components.

modules.version: Modern JavaScript / TypeScript · Vue 3.5 where applicable · browser APIs
modules.cue: Types check your claims. Parsers check outside values.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.content:
## Understand the idea

TypeScript checks code before it runs. It does not validate JSON at runtime. A cast tells the compiler what you claim; it does not turn a string into a number or verify an API response.

A discriminated union uses one field to distinguish valid shapes. A loading state does not need fake rows and an error at the same time. Narrow the union before reading a field that exists only in one variant.

Use unknown for data you have not checked. Keep interfaces small at the component boundary. Prefer a clear union for status to several booleans that allow impossible combinations such as loading=true and finished=true.

sections.title: Follow a concrete example
Trace the execution
sections.content:
## Trace the execution

At compile time, narrowing follows kind. At runtime, a parser checks actual values. Once parsed, UI code can work with the smaller trusted shape. Recheck when a new outside boundary is crossed.

For an exhaustive switch, assign the unreachable value to never. A later added state can then produce a compiler error in code that forgot to handle it.

sections.title: Break it and reason about the repair
sections.content:
## Break it and reason about the repair

Non-null assertions hide absence but do not create a DOM element. any spreads unchecked assumptions across the program. Optional properties can conceal a missing required business decision.

**Remember:** Types check your claims. Parsers check outside values.

modules.title: CSS layout: size, flow, Flexbox, and Grid
modules.outcome: Choose a layout from content behavior and debug overflow instead of adding random widths.
modules.useCase: Support dashboards with sidebars, toolbars, and long technical content.
modules.benefits: Responsive pages that survive real content.
modules.drawbacks: Nested min-size and overflow rules require inspection.
modules.version: Modern JavaScript / TypeScript · Vue 3.5 where applicable · browser APIs
modules.cue: Find the box that refuses to shrink.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.content:
## Understand the idea

Normal flow is the starting point: blocks stack and inline content flows within a line. The box model adds padding and border around content. box-sizing:border-box makes a declared width include padding and border. It does not make every child shrink automatically.

Use Flexbox for one-dimensional distribution: a toolbar, row, or column. Use Grid when rows and columns should align together. A flexible item may refuse to shrink below its min-content size. min-width:0 on the right child or minmax(0,1fr) on a grid track often fixes a long code/title overflow. Find the actual owner before applying it everywhere.

Responsive design follows content constraints. A breakpoint is where this layout stops working, not a universal device category. Use relative sizing, wrapping, and a readable line length. Keep DOM reading order sensible instead of using visual order to repair confusing markup.

sections.title: Follow a concrete example
Trace the execution
sections.content:
## Trace the execution

Inspect the overflowing element's bounding box. Walk to its grid/flex parent. Check min-size, fixed width, padding, and white-space. Change one rule, observe the effect, then remove temporary patches.

A 100vw child plus body padding can overflow. A fixed-height card can cut off translated text. Avoid hiding overflow as the first repair because it can conceal controls or focused content.

sections.title: Break it and reason about the repair
sections.content:
## Break it and reason about the repair

A layout can look correct with short English text and fail with a long title or 200% zoom. overflow:hidden can hide the symptom while clipping important content.

**Remember:** Find the box that refuses to shrink.

exercises.title: Diagnose and repair
exercises.prompt:
## Diagnose and repair

A two-column workspace overflows when a long code sample appears. The right column uses 1fr. Diagnose the min-size boundary and repair it.

Before opening a reference, write your prediction, the exact change, how you would verify it, and why it works. Use synthetic data and a separate lab. State clearly which checks you actually ran.
exercises.solution:
## One valid repair

Use minmax(0,1fr) and/or min-width:0 at the actual flex/grid child. Give the code block its own horizontal scroll. Verify document scroll width at narrow widths, long strings, and zoom; do not simply clip the page.

A different answer can work if it meets the stated rule. Explain the failure timeline and the tradeoff. A product name or a longer answer is not proof.

exercises.title: Change the situation
exercises.prompt:
## Change the situation

The toolbar grows from two actions to six and must work on mobile. What should determine the layout change?

Before opening a reference, write your prediction, the exact change, how you would verify it, and why it works. Use synthetic data and a separate lab. State clearly which checks you actually ran.
exercises.solution:
## One valid transfer

Try wrapping and preserve logical action order. Switch layout when labels and touch targets no longer fit comfortably. Test real labels, keyboard focus, and translated text instead of relying only on a named phone width.

A different answer can work if it meets the stated rule. Explain the failure timeline and the tradeoff. A product name or a longer answer is not proof.

modules.title: One owner for each piece of state
modules.outcome: Separate source state, derived values, URL state, server data, and temporary UI state.
modules.cue: Store facts. Derive views.
modules.version: Portable JavaScript · React hooks · Vue 2/3 comparisons · Next App Router

sections.title: The idea
sections.content:
# The idea

Source state is information you choose to store. Derived state can be calculated from it. If tasks and a filter are stored, visibleTasks can often be derived. Storing both copies creates a synchronization job you may not need.

URL state belongs in the URL when users should bookmark, refresh, or share it, such as search and page. Server state is remote data with freshness and loading concerns. Local UI state includes an open tooltip or unsaved input. A global store is not the default home for everything.

Give each fact one clear owner. Other places read it or send updates through that owner. A cache is another copy with a freshness policy, not a new unquestioned source of truth.

sections.title: A small example
Follow the execution
sections.content:
# Follow the execution

Begin with the user action. Editing a draft changes local unsaved state. Saving asks the server to change persisted state. A successful response updates the cached server record. A derived list recalculates from that cache and the URL filter.

For optimistic UI, record how to undo or reconcile a failed action. If two saves overlap, an old response must not erase a newer edit. A disabled button alone may not cover every caller.

sections.title: What can go wrong
sections.content:
# What can go wrong

Copying props into local state once can make later prop changes invisible. Deriving everything in an effect adds extra updates and stale intermediate renders. Define ownership and reset rules first.

**Memory cue:** Store facts. Derive views.

Close this lesson. Draw the five steps. Explain one failure in your own words before opening Practice.

exercises.title: Find and fix the bug
exercises.prompt:
# Find and fix the bug

A component stores tasks, filter, and visibleTasks. Updating a task forgets to update visibleTasks. Repair the model.

Write: prediction → proposed change → observed evidence → explanation. Run code only in a separate training sandbox. If you did not run it, say so. Submit before opening a reference.
exercises.solution:
# One valid repair

Keep tasks and filter as source state and derive visibleTasks during render/computed evaluation. Store only values that carry independent information. Test changing both the filter and a task without a manual synchronization effect.

**How to check:** If it can be calculated reliably from existing state, storing another copy can create avoidable drift.

Other repairs are acceptable if they satisfy the stated rule. Explain the failure timeline and show a relevant test. Code length and matching keywords are not evidence.

exercises.title: Change one condition
exercises.prompt:
# Change one condition

A delete disappears optimistically, then fails. What must the UI remember?

Write: prediction → proposed change → observed evidence → explanation. Run code only in a separate training sandbox. If you did not run it, say so. Submit before opening a reference.
exercises.solution:
# One valid adaptation

Keep enough information to restore the item or refetch authoritative state. Show failure next to the action and preserve unrelated edits. Handle overlapping deletes/saves by operation identity rather than one global boolean.

**Explain back:** Store facts. Derive views. What changed in the new condition? What would make your answer fail?
