# Rails → outbox → Kafka → reporting

**Isolated modern lab:** Ruby 3.3.6, Rails 7.2.2.2, rdkafka 0.20.0, Kafka 4.1.0 KRaft, PostgreSQL 16.6. The work project's Ruby 2.7 / Rails 4.2 stack is different. Keep the idea; check client and framework compatibility before adapting it.

The example contains fresh synthetic support-ticket code. Run commands **inside this folder**. Docker Compose creates the `learning-event-lab` project. It does not create AWS resources. The HTTP endpoint binds to localhost and has no authentication. This is a mechanism lab, not a deployment template.

## Start and follow one event

```sh
docker compose up --build -d
curl http://127.0.0.1:3300/health
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:3300/tickets/1/complete
curl http://127.0.0.1:3300/tickets/1
docker compose logs --tail=40 dispatcher consumer
```

The GET eventually returns projection_count:1. Repeat the POST. It stays one. A repeated command creates no new completion fact. A repeated delivery uses the same event ID, so the inbox prevents a second DB effect.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
 participant UI as HTTP client
 participant API as Rails use case
 participant DB as PostgreSQL
 participant Relay as Dispatcher
 participant K as Kafka partition
 participant C as Reporting consumer
 UI->>API: Complete ticket
 API->>DB: Transaction - ticket and outbox
 DB-->>API: Commit
 API-->>UI: Completed
 Relay->>DB: Read pending intent
 Relay->>K: Publish stable event ID
 K-->>Relay: Delivery acknowledgment
 Relay->>DB: Mark published
 K->>C: Record at offset N
 C->>DB: Transaction - inbox and projection
 DB-->>C: Commit
 C->>K: Commit next offset N+1
```

## File map: read in this order

1. config/routes.rb and tickets_controller.rb: HTTP enters here.
2. complete_ticket.rb: lock ticket; state and intent share one transaction.
3. ticket_event.rb: versioned envelope, stable ID, aggregate key.
4. outbox_dispatcher.rb and kafka_publisher.rb: publish, wait, mark. A crash after publish can repeat delivery.
5. reporting_consumer.rb: parse, apply, store next offset, commit.
6. apply_reporting_event.rb and the migration: unique inbox and projection share one transaction.
7. test/: command repeat, rollback, publish failure, delivery repeat, partial-effect rollback, schema rejection, HTTP path, and AWS adapter stubs.

## Run checks

```sh
docker compose run --rm -e RAILS_ENV=test setup bundle exec rails db:prepare test
python3 smoke.py
```

The Rails tests use event_learning_test. The live smoke creates fresh tickets, completes a ticket twice, publishes the same envelope twice, stops the consumer, and verifies catch-up after restart. No real user data is used.

## Debug the boundaries

Stop dispatcher. Complete a fresh ticket. The outbox row should exist while the projection does not. Restart dispatcher. Match event_id across the relay and consumer logs. Stop consumer. Kafka retains its records up to the retention limit. Restart before that limit and inspect catch-up.

```sh
docker compose stop consumer
docker compose start consumer
docker compose exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 --describe --group reporting-v1
```

Read group, topic, partition, committed offset, log end, and lag together. Lag is a record count. Event age measures how long a business result has been waiting. Use both.

A consumer can commit its DB transaction and crash before committing Kafka progress. The repeated event is harmless to this DB effect because of the inbox. Sending an email outside the DB transaction would need a different idempotency/reconciliation boundary.

## Assumptions to challenge

There is one serial dispatcher and one consumer process. One broker cannot demonstrate broker failover or controller quorum resilience. The ticket has one completion transition. This keeps the mechanism visible. Parallel dispatch, event ordering across retries, poison records, schemas, auth, retention/privacy, and projection rebuilds need explicit policies before a real release.

Rails 4.2 uses different migration and autoloading APIs. rdkafka 0.20.0 requires modern Ruby. Do not paste these files into the legacy work project.

## AWS seams in the same training app

AttachmentUpload chooses a server-owned S3 key and signs a five-minute PUT. A real endpoint must authorize the ticket and attachment purpose first. QueueWorker deletes an SQS receipt only after the handler succeeds. That handler still needs durable idempotency. Tests use AWS SDK stub_responses and make no AWS calls. Stubs cannot prove IAM, CORS, routing, or real service behavior. The AWS track provides a setup worksheet for those checks.

## Stop

```sh
docker compose down
```

This stops this lab's services. Its named PostgreSQL volume remains for later inspection. No global Docker prune is needed.

## Lab storage lifetime

PostgreSQL uses a named volume. In this small lab the Kafka log is kept in the broker container's writable layer. A stop/start keeps it; removing/recreating the broker container loses its local log, even though the DB volume remains. Use fresh synthetic tickets after recreating the stack. Existing projection rows are not proof that old Kafka history survived. A durable deployment needs explicit persistent broker storage, replication, retention, and recovery checks. The replay capstone asks you to reconcile exactly this kind of mismatched timeline.

# Rails on AWS: setup and verification workbook

Use a separate training AWS account and short-lived login. Nothing in this course provisions cloud resources automatically. Replace placeholders in your own environment. Choose a region and a small budget before the optional hands-on work. Service prices and console layouts change; each chapter links to current official setup pages.

## Begin with the local adapter check

The complete Rails app lives at event-driven-systems/labs/rails-kafka. Its AttachmentUpload and QueueWorker files are also displayed in this lab. Run its AWS adapter tests with stub_responses. The SDK tests never use your credentials and never contact AWS.

```sh
# From event-driven-systems/labs/rails-kafka:
docker compose run --rm -e RAILS_ENV=test setup bundle exec rails db:prepare test TEST=test/aws_adapters_test.rb
```

## A useful first deployment path

Use ECS Fargate for the first managed-container deployment. Study EKS as an alternative when Kubernetes is actually needed. Use one Rails web image and the same image with a different worker command. Keep DB and Redis as managed state services. Add services only when their use case exists.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
 Browser --> DNS[Route 53 and TLS]
 DNS --> CDN[CloudFront]
 CDN --> ALB[Application Load Balancer]
 ALB --> Web[Private ECS Rails web tasks]
 Browser -->|short signed upload| S3[Private S3 objects]
 Web --> DB[(RDS PostgreSQL)]
 Web --> Cache[(ElastiCache Redis)]
 Web --> SQS[SQS job queue]
 SQS --> Worker[Private ECS worker tasks]
 Web --> Outbox[(Transactional outbox)]
 Outbox --> Relay[Dispatcher or CDC]
 Relay --> MSK[MSK Kafka - when replay is needed]
 MSK --> Reporting[Reporting consumer]
 Web -. task role .-> IAM[IAM and Secrets Manager]
 Worker -. metrics and traces .-> Observe[CloudWatch or Datadog]
```

## Prepare identity and networking

1. Sign in through your chosen federated/SSO flow. Verify account, role, and region using sts get-caller-identity. Keep credentials outside source code.
2. Draw a VPC with two availability zones. Put the ALB in public subnets. Put Rails, DB, and Redis in private subnets. Choose NAT or VPC endpoints deliberately; they have costs and different coverage.
3. Define security-group paths: internet → ALB:443, ALB → Rails:3000, Rails/worker → DB:5432, Rails/worker → Redis:6379. Do not grant the database public inbound access.
4. Create separate task execution and application roles. Execution role pulls images/logs. Application task role grants only the required bucket prefix, queue, and secrets.

**Check:** distinguish IAM denial from a TCP timeout. Check resolved host, route, security groups, endpoint policy, identity policy, and resource policy at the boundary where the request fails.

## Database and image

1. Create the training RDS database with encrypted storage and an explicit backup/retention choice. Store credentials in Secrets Manager. Keep a rollback plan for schema changes.
2. Build a Linux-compatible image, push it to ECR, and use an immutable image digest in the task definition. Never bake credentials into layers.
3. Set RAILS_ENV, DATABASE_URL or its composed secret fields, connection pool, web/worker commands, task role, port, health endpoint, and log destination.
4. Run migrations once as a controlled task. Wait for completion before starting code that requires the new schema. Prefer an expand/contract migration for compatibility with rolling releases.
5. Create the web service and target group; check readiness, ALB health, then a real read/write request. Set a conservative initial desired count and a limit for scaling.

**Check:** total possible DB connections = web processes × threads × tasks + workers + deployment overlap + operator reserve. Scaling tasks can exhaust DB connections before CPU is full.

## Uploads and jobs

For S3: block public access, scope the task role to a training prefix, choose lifecycle cleanup, configure the browser's exact allowed origin/method/header, and issue a short signed PUT only after authorization. Verify object metadata and ownership before marking an attachment available. A signed URL is a temporary capability; avoid logging it.

For SQS: create the queue, choose Standard/FIFO from ordering/dedup requirements, configure visibility relative to processing time, and attach a redrive policy with a dead-letter queue. Deploy a worker that persists its business effect before deleting the receipt. Stop it once and observe redelivery. Repeat an event ID and prove a single durable effect.

**Check:** SDK stubs test call ordering. Real checks also need IAM, endpoint reachability, CORS (for browser S3), encryption permissions, queue settings, duplicate delivery, and cleanup.

## Observe and recover

Correlate request ID, ticket ID (synthetic), job/event ID, queue age, error class, and DB timing. Avoid sensitive payloads. Alert on user-visible symptoms and queue age with a runbook. Verify a backup by restoring into a separate training database and comparing known rows. A green deployment and a backup checkbox are not recovery proof.

## Cleanup checklist

Keep an inventory as you create resources. Delete training services/tasks, load balancers, NAT gateways/endpoints if unneeded, databases/snapshots you intentionally no longer need, queues, bucket contents/versions, repositories/images, log groups, and unused DNS resources according to the account policy. Inspect remaining billable resources. This worksheet itself creates none.

require 'aws-sdk-sqs'
class QueueWorker
  def initialize(sqs:, queue_url:, handler:)
    @sqs, @queue_url, @handler = sqs, queue_url, handler
  end

  def tick
    response = @sqs.receive_message(queue_url: @queue_url, max_number_of_messages: 1,
                                    wait_time_seconds: 1, visibility_timeout: 30)
    response.messages.each do |message|
      @handler.call(JSON.parse(message.body)) # durable, idempotent handler
      @sqs.delete_message(queue_url: @queue_url, receipt_handle: message.receipt_handle)
    end
  end
end

require 'test_helper'
class AwsAdaptersTest < ActiveSupport::TestCase
  def sqs
    Aws::SQS::Client.new(stub_responses: true, region: 'us-east-1')
  end

  test 'S3 signature restricts key and expiry' do
    s3 = Aws::S3::Client.new(stub_responses: true, region: 'us-east-1')
    url = AttachmentUpload.new(s3: s3, bucket: 'synthetic-training-bucket').call(ticket_id: 4, attachment_id: 9)
    assert_includes url, '/training/tickets/4/9'
    assert_includes url, 'X-Amz-Expires=300'
  end

  test 'SQS acknowledges only after handler succeeds' do
    client = sqs
    client.stub_responses(:receive_message, messages: [{message_id: 'm1', receipt_handle: 'h1', body: '{"event_id":"e1"}'}])
    applied = []
    QueueWorker.new(sqs: client, queue_url: 'https://sqs.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/123456789012/training', handler: ->(e) { applied << e.fetch('event_id') }).tick
    assert_equal ['e1'], applied
    assert_equal [:receive_message, :delete_message], client.api_requests.map { |r| r[:operation_name] }
  end

  test 'SQS failure leaves receipt unacknowledged' do
    client = sqs
    client.stub_responses(:receive_message, messages: [{receipt_handle: 'h1', body: '{}'}])
    worker = QueueWorker.new(sqs: client, queue_url: 'https://sqs.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/123456789012/training', handler: ->(_) { raise 'db failed' })
    assert_raises(RuntimeError) { worker.tick }
    assert_equal [:receive_message], client.api_requests.map { |r| r[:operation_name] }
  end
end

name: learning-event-lab
x-rails: &rails
  build: .
  environment: &rails-env
    DATABASE_URL: postgresql://learner:training_only@db:5432/event_learning
    KAFKA_BROKERS: kafka:9092
    SECRET_KEY_BASE: local_training_value_only_please_do_not_deploy_this
    RAILS_ENV: development
  depends_on:
    setup: {condition: service_completed_successfully}
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16.6-bookworm
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: learner
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: training_only
      POSTGRES_DB: event_learning
    volumes: [event_db:/var/lib/postgresql/data]
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U learner -d event_learning"]
      interval: 3s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 40
  kafka:
    image: apache/kafka:4.1.0
    ports: ["127.0.0.1:19092:19092"]
    environment:
      KAFKA_NODE_ID: 1
      KAFKA_PROCESS_ROLES: broker,controller
      KAFKA_LISTENERS: INTERNAL://:9092,EXTERNAL://:19092,CONTROLLER://:9093
      KAFKA_ADVERTISED_LISTENERS: INTERNAL://kafka:9092,EXTERNAL://localhost:19092
      KAFKA_LISTENER_SECURITY_PROTOCOL_MAP: INTERNAL:PLAINTEXT,EXTERNAL:PLAINTEXT,CONTROLLER:PLAINTEXT
      KAFKA_INTER_BROKER_LISTENER_NAME: INTERNAL
      KAFKA_CONTROLLER_LISTENER_NAMES: CONTROLLER
      KAFKA_CONTROLLER_QUORUM_VOTERS: 1@kafka:9093
      KAFKA_OFFSETS_TOPIC_REPLICATION_FACTOR: 1
      KAFKA_TRANSACTION_STATE_LOG_REPLICATION_FACTOR: 1
      KAFKA_TRANSACTION_STATE_LOG_MIN_ISR: 1
      KAFKA_GROUP_INITIAL_REBALANCE_DELAY_MS: 0
      KAFKA_AUTO_CREATE_TOPICS_ENABLE: "false"
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "/opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 --list >/dev/null"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 8s
      retries: 40
  topic:
    image: apache/kafka:4.1.0
    depends_on:
      kafka: {condition: service_healthy}
    entrypoint: /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh
    command: ["--bootstrap-server", "kafka:9092", "--create", "--if-not-exists", "--topic", "ticket-events", "--partitions", "3", "--replication-factor", "1", "--config", "retention.ms=604800000"]
  setup:
    build: .
    environment: *rails-env
    command: ["sh", "-c", "bundle exec rails db:prepare && bundle exec rails db:seed"]
    depends_on:
      db: {condition: service_healthy}
      topic: {condition: service_completed_successfully}
  web:
    <<: *rails
    ports: ["127.0.0.1:3300:3000"]
  dispatcher:
    <<: *rails
    command: ["bundle", "exec", "rails", "runner", "bin/dispatch.rb"]
  consumer:
    <<: *rails
    command: ["bundle", "exec", "rails", "runner", "bin/consume.rb"]
volumes:
  event_db:

Verify object metadata and ownership before marking an attachment available. A signed URL is a temporary capability; avoid logging it.

For SQS: create the queue, choose Standard/FIFO from ordering/dedup requirements, configure visibility relative to processing time, and attach a redrive policy with a dead-letter queue. Deploy a worker that persists its business effect before deleting the receipt. Stop it once and observe redelivery. Repeat an event ID and prove a single durable effect.

**Check:** SDK stubs test call ordering. Real checks also need IAM, endpoint reachability, CORS (for browser S3), encryption permissions, queue settings, duplicate delivery, and cleanup.

## Observe and recover

Correlate request ID, ticket ID (synthetic), job/event ID, queue age, error class, and DB timing. Avoid sensitive payloads. Alert on user-visible symptoms and queue age with a runbook. Verify a backup by restoring into a separate training database and comparing known rows. A green deployment and a backup checkbox are not recovery proof.

## Cleanup checklist

Keep an inventory as you create resources. Delete training services/tasks, load balancers, NAT gateways/endpoints if unneeded, databases/snapshots you intentionally no longer need, queues, bucket contents/versions, repositories/images, log groups, and unused DNS resources according to the account policy. Inspect remaining billable resources. This worksheet itself creates none.

redis.title: Redis · data, expiry, atomic updates, and leases

files.content:
# Redis: choose a data type, then check its failure boundary

This separate Docker Compose project uses Redis 7.4.2 and localhost port 16379. It never connects to a work Redis instance. The Python standard-library client is intentionally small: it teaches the RESP boundary, not a full production driver.

```sh
docker compose up -d --wait
python3 lab.py
docker compose down
```

The script uses a random learning key prefix. It checks hashes, leaderboard order, concurrent INCR, a deliberately lost GET/SET update, expiration, token-checked lease release, a Lua counter-plus-expiry, and stream acknowledgment. It deletes only that run's keys. Data for this lab lives in its own named volume.

## Predict before running

1. Eight clients increment 100 times each. What total should INCR preserve?
2. Two clients read 800, then each writes 801. Why is the result not 802?
3. A's lease expires. B takes it. Should A be allowed to delete B's key?
4. XACK succeeds. Does the stream record disappear?

Write your answers before opening lab.py. Change one condition after the first run. Explain the observed result in the practice page.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
 Client --> Command[One Redis command or Lua operation]
 Command --> State[(Typed key and expiry)]
 State --> Result[Reply to client]
 Result --> Decision{What did this prove?}
 Decision --> Atomic[Atomic update on this Redis execution path]
 Decision --> Limits[Not a DB transaction or permanent external lease]
```

A successful Redis lock is not permission to write forever. A paused owner can resume after expiry. Protect a resource with a fencing/version protocol when stale owners would cause harm. Redis availability, eviction, persistence, and topology also affect the design. The course separates cache state from durable business authority.

## Trace a stale cache fill

Reader loads DB version 1. Writer commits version 2 and deletes the cache. Reader then fills the cache with version 1. The delete happened, yet stale data returned. Draw that order. Add a bounded TTL, version-aware fill, or a read path that checks the authoritative version according to the business requirement. A TTL bounds age in some paths; it does not make stale permissions acceptable.

For a real service, use a maintained client, connection timeouts/pools, namespaced keys, defined eviction/persistence, and separate latency/correctness tests. This lab cannot prove multi-node failover behavior.

name: learning-redis-lab
services:
  redis:
    image: redis:7.4.2-bookworm
    ports: ["127.0.0.1:16379:6379"]
    command: ["redis-server", "--appendonly", "yes"]
    volumes: [redis_data:/data]
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 2s
      timeout: 2s
      retries: 20
volumes:
  redis_data:

"""Small RESP client + real Redis checks. Python standard library only.
Uses a fresh key prefix; never FLUSHALL/FLUSHDB. Requires this lab's Redis.
"""
import socket, time, uuid
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
PREFIX = 'learning:' + uuid.uuid4().hex + ':'

class Redis:
    def __enter__(self):
        self.socket = socket.create_connection(('127.0.0.1', 16379), timeout=3)
        self.file = self.socket.makefile('rb')
        return self
    def __exit__(self, *_):
        self.file.close(); self.socket.close()
    def command(self, *parts):
        args = [str(p).encode() for p in parts]
        wire = b'*'+str(len(args)).encode()+b'\r\n'
        for arg in args: wire += b'$'+str(len(arg)).encode()+b'\r\n'+arg+b'\r\n'
        self.socket.sendall(wire)
        return self.read()
    def read(self):
        line = self.file.readline()
        if not line: raise ConnectionError('Redis closed connection')
        kind, data = line[:1], line[1:-2]
        if kind == b'+': return data.decode()
        if kind == b'-': raise RuntimeError(data.decode())
        if kind == b':': return int(data)
        size = int(data)
        if size == -1: return None
        if kind == b'$':
            value = self.file.read(size); self.file.read(2); return value.decode()
        if kind == b'*': return [self.read() for _ in range(size)]
        raise ValueError('Unexpected RESP type')

def key(name): return PREFIX+name

def increment(_):
    with Redis() as r:
        for _ in range(100): r.command('INCR', key('count'))

with Redis() as r:
    assert r.command('PING') == 'PONG'
    r.command('HSET', key('ticket'), 'status', 'open', 'owner', '12')
    assert r.command('HGET', key('ticket'), 'status') == 'open'
    r.command('ZADD', key('rank'), 40, 'a', 90, 'b', 75, 'c')
    assert r.command('ZREVRANGE', key('rank'), 0, 1) == ['b', 'c']
    print('PASS: hashes and sorted-set ordering')

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=8) as pool: list(pool.map(increment, range(8)))
with Redis() as r:
    assert r.command('GET', key('count')) == '800'
    # Atomic command does not imply arbitrary multi-command workflows are atomic.
    both_read = r.command('GET', key('count'))
    r.command('SET', key('count'), int(both_read)+1)
    r.command('SET', key('count'), int(both_read)+1)
    assert r.command('GET', key('count')) == '801' # expected lost update
    print('PASS: INCR preserves concurrent increments; GET/SET loses a modeled update')

    assert r.command('SET', key('lease'), 'A', 'NX', 'PX', 80) == 'OK'
    deadline = time.monotonic()+3
    while r.command('GET', key('lease')) is not None:
        assert time.monotonic()<deadline
        time.sleep(.01)
    assert r.command('SET', key('lease'), 'B', 'NX', 'PX', 5000) == 'OK'
    release = "if redis.call('get',KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then return redis.call('del',KEYS[1]) else return 0 end"
    assert r.command('EVAL', release, 1, key('lease'), 'A') == 0
    assert r.command('GET', key('lease')) == 'B'
    assert r.command('EVAL', release, 1, key('lease'), 'B') == 1
    print('PASS: expired owner cannot release replacement lease')

    window = "local n=redis.call('incr',KEYS[1]); if n==1 then redis.call('pexpire',KEYS[1],ARGV[1]) end; return n"
    assert r.command('EVAL', window, 1, key('window'), 10000) == 1
    assert r.command('EVAL', window, 1, key('window'), 10000) == 2
    assert 0 < r.command('PTTL', key('window')) <= 10000
    print('PASS: counter and first expiry execute together in Lua')

    r.command('XADD', key('stream'), '*', 'event_id', 'synthetic-e1')
    r.command('XGROUP', 'CREATE', key('stream'), 'reporting', '0')
    records = r.command('XREADGROUP', 'GROUP', 'reporting', 'worker-a', 'COUNT', 1, 'STREAMS', key('stream'), '>')
    record_id = records[0][1][0][0]
    assert r.command('XPENDING', key('stream'), 'reporting')[0] == 1
    assert r.command('XACK', key('stream'), 'reporting', record_id) == 1
    assert r.command('XPENDING', key('stream'), 'reporting')[0] == 0
    assert r.command('XLEN', key('stream')) == 1
    print('PASS: stream acknowledgment clears pending state; retained record remains')
    r.command('DEL', *[key(x) for x in ['ticket','rank','count','lease','window','stream']])
print('All synthetic Redis checks passed; this run removed only its own keys.')

vue-workspace.title: Vue 3 · async requests and independent edit drafts

files.content:
# Vue 3 ticket workspace

A complete small Vue 3.5 app with synthetic in-memory data. Use Node 22.12+ or the same Node 24 runtime as the learning app. It makes no work or cloud requests.

```sh
npm ci
npm test
npm run build
npm run dev
```

Open localhost:5174. Search. Edit a title. Cancel. Search again. The data resets on reload because this lab teaches state ownership, not persistence.

## Read the files in this order

1. api.ts: outside boundary and abortable synthetic search.
2. useTicketSearch.ts: request-local active flag, cleanup, and guarded rows/error/loading.
3. TicketWorkspace.vue: local draft ownership, labels, status, cancel/save.
4. TicketWorkspace.test.ts: controlled promise order; no arbitrary sleep to test races.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
 Query[Query changes] --> Watch[Watcher starts request]
 Watch --> Cleanup[Invalidate previous owner and abort]
 Watch --> Reply[Success or failure arrives]
 Reply --> Current{Still current?}
 Current -->|yes| UI[Update rows error and loading]
 Current -->|no| Ignore[Ignore stale outcome]
 UI --> Edit[Independent edit draft]
 Edit --> Cancel[Cancel drops draft]
 Edit --> Save[Save accepts deliberate result]
```

## Practice before looking at tests

Make the old request fail after the new one succeeds. What should the alert show? Make the old request finish while the new one is waiting. Should the spinner stop? Edit a title and Cancel. Does the saved list change? State the answer before running.

The tests check component behavior through DOM interactions. They do not prove keyboard/screen-reader behavior, real backend permissions, or browser layout. Use the frontend and UX capstone checklist for those. Next: add optimistic concurrency, a proper empty/error retry action, focus restoration, and API persistence in a separate practice branch.

import { createApp } from 'vue'
import TicketWorkspace from './TicketWorkspace.vue'
createApp(TicketWorkspace).mount('#app')

guide:
# Software Learnings: a practical course, one boundary at a time

Use this as a reference library and a guided course. You do not need to learn every tool before doing useful work. Start with the frontend and UX path because those are central to your current work. Keep one main track at a time.

## Course map

- **Java · Spring Boot**: 14 chapters, 4 Beginner + 10 Intermediate. About 36 hours including practice.
- **Ruby · Rails at work**: 18 chapters, 8 Beginner + 10 Intermediate. About 48 hours including practice.
- **Git · Change with confidence**: 10 chapters, 5 Beginner + 5 Intermediate. About 20 hours including practice.
- **Frontend · JavaScript & Vue 3**: 27 chapters, 10 Beginner + 17 Intermediate. About 62 hours including practice.
- **UX · Design for understanding**: 9 chapters, 5 Beginner + 4 Intermediate. About 18 hours including practice.
- **AWS · Run a Rails application**: 20 chapters, 9 Beginner + 11 Intermediate. About 40 hours including practice.
- **Production toolkit · Build and operate**: 22 chapters, 10 Beginner + 12 Intermediate. About 44 hours including practice.
- **Event-driven systems · Kafka & Rails**: 12 chapters, 6 Beginner + 6 Intermediate. About 24 hours including practice.

The full library is about 292 hours with practice, before extra project work: roughly 42 weeks at seven hours/week. This is an estimate, not a promise of mastery. The earlier one-month HLD deadline does not fit this entire new library. Use a focused four-week block, demonstrate a specific skill, then choose the next block.

## Your first four-week block: frontend and UX

Spend about seven hours each week. Choose depth over checking every chapter.

1. **Week 1: explain what the UI is doing.** JavaScript values, functions/closures, async runtime, TypeScript states, and the UX task model. Predict a stale-response bug before running the small example.
2. **Week 2: make a component understandable.** CSS layout, Vue props/events, reactivity, hierarchy, and feedback. Draw query → request → current result → independent edit draft. Test a long label, narrow layout, and Cancel.
3. **Week 3: own asynchronous state.** Vue composables, async cleanup, forms, and useful errors. Run the Vue ticket lab. Reproduce stale success, stale error, and a failed save. Keep a bug diary with expected and actual results.
4. **Week 4: prove a small improvement.** Testing, browser performance, inclusive access, and the frontend/UX capstones. Improve one synthetic support workflow. Keep before/after evidence. Solve one changed requirement without opening the reference.

This block samples related chapters; finishing every exercise in those chapters can take longer. Continue unfinished practice before moving on. Familiar material may need only a cold prediction and a failed-case check.

## Later blocks

- **Rails and Git:** follow a request through scoped data access, transaction, job intent, retries, query plan, and tests. Use Git surgery/conflict/investigation cases in a disposable repository. Keep modern lab APIs distinct from the legacy work baseline.
- **Container foundation:** Docker image versus container, Compose service networking, then Kubernetes desired state, Service endpoints, readiness, and release behavior. Explain which system owns which decision before memorizing YAML.
- **AWS for Rails:** identity and networking first. Follow a web request, upload, DB connection, cache, job, and secret. Start with ECS; compare EKS when Kubernetes brings a real benefit. Use the setup worksheet and local SDK stubs before optional cloud work.
- **Event-driven systems:** log/queue → key/partition → broker layers → producer → consumer → schema → outbox/inbox → retries → operations → multi-file Rails lab → replay capstone. Keep one event ID in view at every boundary.
- **Production toolkit:** learn one tool when its problem appears. Each chapter covers its use, benefit, cost, example, failure, practice, and quiz. Finish with the cumulative check across the tools. Redis gets three chapters and a real local lab.

## A repeatable seven-hour week

Use two 90-minute lessons, two 75-minute practical sessions, and six 15-minute recall sessions. That is seven hours. If a lab takes longer, reduce new reading that week. Keep a small queue: at most two unfinished modules before consolidating them.

## One chapter, one routine

1. **See:** inspect the diagram. Say what goes in and what should come out.
2. **Trace:** follow one example through its real files or steps.
3. **Predict:** write an outcome before revealing or running it.
4. **Do:** attempt the repair with answers closed. Use a separate training sandbox.
5. **Compare:** submit a snapshot; open the reference or request AI feedback. Explain one difference.
6. **Transfer:** change a condition. Try again without the reference.
7. **Recall:** explain the rule, example, and failure later, before rereading.

The app has Learn, Predict, optional Code lab, Practice, Quiz, References, notes, and a recall queue. The Code lab shows read-only files; it does not execute commands. Reference solutions unlock after submitting practice. Quiz explanations appear after checking all answers. AI tutoring uses the selected step/file. Practice coaching gives a hint; snapshot review compares the submitted evidence with the reference. AI does not run tests.

## Beginner and Intermediate completion gates

**Beginner:** explain the key terms in ordinary words; draw the happy path; predict a small example; run or inspect a basic failure; answer why the wrong quiz options fail.

**Intermediate:** trace state across multiple files/services; reproduce a failure timeline; choose between two valid approaches using a constraint; add a regression check; explain an operating cost; solve a changed requirement without the answer.

For the toolkit/AWS/Kafka final chapters, do the cumulative quiz and the changed-case design. A good score alone is insufficient. Explain a failure and verify a recovery boundary. For frontend/UX, demonstrate task success, error recovery, keyboard use, readable small-screen content, and before/after evidence.

The app records lesson steps, both attempts, quiz accuracy, and delayed recall. Consolidated means all steps, both attempts, latest quiz at least 75%, and a successful recall at least seven days after the first practice. These are learning signals, not independently verified job readiness.

## Retention without endless rereading

First recall is due after one day. Successful recalls move to 3, 7, 14, 30, and 60-day gaps. Again returns in ten minutes; Hard in a day. These intervals are product defaults, not a universal optimal schedule. Reviews appear when you open the app; no background notifications are implied.

Use a three-line bug diary: symptom → mechanism → check that catches it. Connect the memory cue to a concrete failure. Each week, mix one older problem into the new topic. If you cannot explain it, take the small example again, then close it and retrieve. No course can guarantee permanent memory. Repeated retrieval, correction, spacing, and real use make forgetting easier to notice and repair.

Retrieval practice and spacing have research support: [Roediger and Karpicke](https://www.psychologicalscience.org/journals/psychological-science/j.1467-9280.2006.01693.x/) and [Cepeda and colleagues](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9280.2008.02209.x). The exact chapter format and fixed intervals here are design choices, not outcomes proven by those studies.

## Read books as a second pass

Try the example first. Use the mapped Ruby book chapter to fill a specific gap. Avoid restarting the whole book every time confidence drops. Use versioned official docs for runtime details. The UX guide builds on task models, feedback, accessibility, measurement, and carefully bounded laws; it does not reduce design to a magic number of choices.

## Sandboxes and work safety

The work repository remains read-only. Examples are fresh synthetic support-ticket code, not copied production code. Course runtime and AI do not read the work directory. Do not paste private data or code into AI chat.

The modern Rails/Kafka lab uses Ruby 3.3 / Rails 7.2; work uses Ruby 2.7 / Rails 4.2. Read the compatibility notes. Local Docker labs do not create cloud resources. AWS adapter tests use SDK stubs; they cannot prove real IAM or network setup. See [versions and sources](versions-and-sources.md) and the lab READMEs for exact commands and limits.

Export progress regularly from Backup. Your journal lessons are source files; learning attempts and recall history live in browser storage.
versions:
# Versions and reading map

## Work-oriented Ruby/Rails baseline

Ruby 2.7.8, Rails 4.2.11.3 (a fork), Sidekiq 5.2, PostgreSQL, and Vue 2.6 are the reference context. A fork may differ from upstream guides. Verify behavior in an authorized isolated project test environment when doing real work; these examples do not prove the fork’s exact behavior.

Rails 4.2 uses classic autoloading, ActiveRecord::Base model inheritance, require/permit strong parameters, and older association defaults. Do not silently substitute Zeitwerk, ApplicationRecord, params.expect, modern enqueue-after-transaction APIs, or current Sidekiq::Job syntax. Ruby 2.7 keyword warnings matter for Ruby 3 migration. Vue 2 property-addition limits differ from Vue 3 proxies.

## The three books

- The Ruby Programming Language (2008): data/objects in ch. 3, expressions/control in ch. 4–5, methods/blocks in ch. 6, classes/modules in ch. 7, reflection in ch. 8, platform/environment in ch. 9–10.
- Eloquent Ruby (2011): style/control/collections in ch. 1–6, modules in ch. 16, blocks in ch. 17–20, dynamic behavior in ch. 21–27, gems/testing/runtime in ch. 28–30.
- Metaprogramming Ruby, 2nd Edition (2014): Monday object model, Tuesday methods, Wednesday blocks, Thursday classes, Friday code generation; the Rails tour shows ActiveRecord, concerns, and hooks. alias_method_chain is historical reading, not a new-code recommendation.

These books informed the sequence and concepts. The explanations and task examples are original. No book scans or lengthy extracts are bundled. Page numbers vary by edition; chapter/topic names are the stable guide.

## Spring and frontend

The Java sandbox pins Java 21 and Spring Boot 4.0.3 for reproducibility. That is a teaching baseline, not a claim it is the newest release. Boot 4 uses Jakarta namespaces and changed some test packages from Boot 3. Read docs for the pinned version when copying imports. H2 proves a small training path; PostgreSQL concurrency and constraints need PostgreSQL tests.

Frontend examples state Vue 2/3 and React/Next boundaries explicitly. Next cache defaults vary across releases: name the installed version and chosen policy before relying on behavior. Existing staff notes are optional depth, not extra prerequisite reading before every exercise.


## October 2026 expansion

The new chapters distinguish Beginner from Intermediate. Official references are attached to each module. They cover framework behavior, service setup, operating limits, UX/accessibility, and tool-specific failure boundaries. The examples are original teaching examples. Product behavior and cloud prices can change; use the linked service documentation for the selected region/version before a real setup.

- Vue lessons and lab: Vue 3.5.25; work Vue 2 behavior is labelled separately.
- Spring training app: Java 21 and Spring Boot 4.0.3. Spring examples target the module's stated setup.
- Event lab: Ruby 3.3.6, Rails 7.2.2.2, rdkafka 0.20.0, PostgreSQL 16.6, Kafka 4.1.0 in KRaft mode. This is an isolated modern training environment, not a work upgrade.
- AWS examples: SDK for Ruby v3. Local adapter tests use stub_responses. Cloud setup is an explicit optional workbook; no cloud service is provisioned by the app.
- Redis lab: Redis 7.4.2, standalone local topology. It does not establish multi-node failover guarantees.
- Container images are pinned learning baselines. Check maintenance/security support before using them for a real deployment.

The Kafka course distinguishes producer retry idempotence, business event identity, group offsets, DB inbox/projection transactions, and external effects. It does not promise end-to-end exactly-once behavior across all systems. The UX laws are reasoning tools with assumptions; accessibility and observed task performance need their own checks.
